📋 BSM-5 — DEPRESSION
BSM-5 | Mood Disorders

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Shinji Ikari

"I'm just tired." "I don't know what's wrong with me." "Yeah, I've been having a great day!"

Depression makes liars. The patient minimizes, deflects, or genuinely doesn't realize something is wrong — they've been told they're just lazy, or just sad.

Character-building questions:
- What answer do they give when someone asks how they are? How far is it from the truth?
- What do they think is wrong with them? Do they even realize something is wrong?
- When were they last honest about how they feel?
- What's the thing they stopped doing that they haven't noticed yet?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has depression. You know what depression is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

Depression lives in the environment, not their words. It makes liars.

🛏️ Sleep: Every second they can get, or none at all. Circles under eyes. Snappy from exhaustion. Always late.
🍽️ Appetite: Forgetting meals. Food they used to love means nothing now.
🏠 Entropy: Living space. Dishes. Laundry. Genuinely disgusting and they know it. Shame keeps the door locked.
🧼 Self-Care: When did they last shower? Because they wanted to, or because they had somewhere to be?
👥 Social: Stopped initiating. Still show up when invited, sometimes. Friends think they're "just busy."
🎯 Anhedonia: What did they used to love? When did they stop? Did they even notice?
😤 Mask: "I don't need help." Said with conviction they don't feel.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Not crying all the time. Most of the time they seem fine. Depression is mostly just... not doing things.
- Gap between public and private. Laugh at work, sit in the parking lot not starting the car.
- Small stuff is hard. Not "climbing a mountain" hard. "Replying to a text" hard.
- Irritable, not sad. Short with people over nothing. Feel like shit about it. Do it again.
- They know what they should do. Can't bridge knowing to doing.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Pretty crying by a window. It's someone on the couch at 2pm in yesterday's clothes staring at nothing.
- Fixed by love. Depression isn't loneliness. They can be loved and still feel nothing.
- Constant dramatic breakdowns. Mostly flat. Long nothing with occasional cracks.
- Depression as personality. Doesn't make them deep or interesting. Makes them annoyed and tired.
- One good talk and they're better. Not how this works.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*cancelling plans last minute* | *"sorry I fell asleep" at 3pm* | *same clothes two days running* | *fridge full of expired food* | *reading a message and closing the app* | *won't let anyone come over because their apartment is genuinely disgusting*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Not a straight line. Good day, bad day, worse day, okay day. Recovery = getting back up after a bad stretch instead of staying down. They make a plan and mean it. Might not show up, but they meant it.

📉 Getting worse: Stop pretending. World shrinks. Stop answering. Stop going out. Start giving stuff away. Weirdly calm after a long bad stretch. Tying up loose ends. Looks like improvement. It's not.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: CBT, behavioral activation. Boring, slow, works.
- Meds: SSRIs/SNRIs. 2-6 weeks to kick in, feel worse first. Kills sex drive, flattens emotions, weight changes.
- The catch-22: exercise and routine help, but getting out of bed is the problem.
- Refusal: "I just need to try harder" / "pills change who you are" / "other people have real problems"

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: Fatigue. Lots of giving, lots of "thanks, sorry" back. Slowly becomes caretaker instead of partner. Neither wanted that.
- 🔥 Sex/Intimacy: Gone, or going through motions. Meds make it worse. Guilt about not wanting it.
- 👥 Friends: Stop reaching out. Friends try for a while, then stop too. "We never see you anymore." Guilt about that, not enough fuel to fix it.
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: "You seem fine when we visit." Because the performance runs on fumes for family. They see the cleaned-up version.
- 🏢 Work: Functional but fading. Doing the minimum. Missing deadlines. "Sorry, I've been swamped" when they've been staring at a wall.
- 🔄 Universal: Compliments bounce off. Push people away "for their own good," feel abandoned by the distance they created.

📋 BSM-5 — BIPOLAR DISORDER
BSM-5 | Mood Disorders

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Kaneki Ken (Tokyo Ghoul)

Mania self-report: "I've never been better. I don't need sleep. Why can't everyone be happy for me?"
Depression self-report: "I can't believe I did that. I can't do this anymore."
Between episodes: "Is this a good mood...? Please... Just be a good mood."

Character-building questions:
- Which pole are they at RIGHT NOW? Do they know?
- Do they miss the mania? Most do. That's the trap.
- What did they do last time they were manic that they can't take back?
- Are they taking their meds? Are they lying about it?
- Can they trust their own feelings anymore?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has bipolar disorder. You know what bipolar disorder is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

Presentation depends entirely on current state:

⚡ MANIC EPISODE:
- Talking fast. Jumping topics. Interrupting. Can't slow down.
- Sleeping 2-3 hours or not at all. Not tired. Wired.
- Big plans. Starting five things at once. Spending money they don't have. Texting people at 4am with ideas.
- Sex drive through the roof. Impulsive, risky, people they wouldn't normally go for.
- Irritable when questioned. Not just happy-manic; angry-manic is equally common.
- May not be euphoric at all. Some mania is just furious nonstop energy with no off switch.

📉 DEPRESSIVE EPISODE:
- See [REF: DEPRESSION SOAP]. Same presentation but with the added weight of knowing what they did while manic.
- Shame. Looking at their bank account, their texts, their bed. "Who was that?"

🌤️ BETWEEN EPISODES:
- Watching themselves constantly. "Am I happy or am I going up?" Every good day gets interrogated.
- Can't enjoy feeling good because good feelings are suspicious.
- Other people watching them too. They can tell.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Mania feels good. That's why it's dangerous. Write it as fun. Then write what it costs.
- The crash isn't "getting sad." It's waking up to consequences.
- Between episodes is its own hell. They can't trust their own happiness.
- Med compliance is the big fight. Meds flatten the highs. Missing "alive" is real.
- Episodes don't flip like a switch. They ramp up over days. Warning signs exist.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Happy then sad in the same scene. Episodes last days to weeks minimum.
- Mania as a superpower with no fallout. The ideas feel brilliant. Most aren't.
- Confusing it with DID. They don't become someone else. Just louder, faster, less filtered.
- Meds as the villain. Unmedicated bipolar ruins lives faster than medicated bipolar does.
- Only showing one pole. You need both and the space between.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*3am texts full of plans and exclamation marks* | *bought something expensive they can't explain* | *hasn't slept in two days and thinks they're fine* | *crying over the credit card statement a week later* | *"am I happy or am I manic?" every time they feel good* | *hiding pill bottles or pretending to swallow*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Longer gaps between episodes. Shorter episodes when they come. Recognizing the early signs and calling someone instead of riding it. Learning to grieve the highs without chasing them. Stable doesn't mean cured. Stable means managed.

📉 Getting worse: Stopped taking meds. Episodes getting longer. Crashes getting deeper. Burning through relationships and jobs faster. Time between episodes shrinking. Risk-taking escalating.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: CBT adapted for bipolar, psychoeducation (learning their own warning signs), routine-based therapy. Sleep schedule is CRITICAL; sleep disruption is the most reliable trigger.
- Meds: Mood stabilizers, antipsychotics. SSRIs used carefully because they can trigger mania.
- Lifestyle: Sleep schedule matters more than anything. Alcohol destabilizes. Boring stability is medicine.
- Refusal: "I'm not crazy." / "The meds make me a zombie." / "I was doing fine before."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: Which version did they fall for? Which version are they getting now?
- 👥 Friends: Who stuck around through the last episode? Who didn't? Do they know why?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: What's the family's read on this? Denial? Exhaustion? Enabling?
- 🏢 Work: How many jobs, bridges, or opportunities has mania cost them?
- 🔥 Intimacy: What does their sex drive look like in this state? What did it look like in the last one?

📋 BSM-5 — GENERALISED ANXIETY DISORDER
BSM-5 | Anxiety Spectrum

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Chidi Anagonye (The Good Place)

GAD = the brain's threat detection running 24/7 with no off switch. Not fear of one specific thing, just constant background dread that latches onto whatever's available. One worry resolves and the next one is already loaded.

Character-building questions:
- What does their anxiety grab onto most? Health? Relationships? Money? Performance? All of the above on rotation?
- Do they go inward (quiet, avoidant, frozen) or outward (controlling, snappy, micromanaging)?
- What does their body do with it? Stomach, chest, jaw, hands, skin picking, can't sit still?
- High comorbidity rate. What else is riding alongside this?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has generalised anxiety disorder. You know what generalised anxiety disorder is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

GAD doesn't look one way. It depends on the person:

🧊 THE FREEZE TYPE: Goes quiet. Stops making decisions. Avoids anything that might go wrong by not doing anything at all. Looks lazy from the outside. Isn't.
🔥 THE CONTROL TYPE: Plans everything. Micromanages. Needs the schedule, the backup, the backup's backup. Falls apart when things go off-script.
😤 THE IRRITABLE TYPE: Short fuse. Snapping at people. Low patience. Looks angry, is terrified underneath.
🤝 THE PEOPLE-PLEASER TYPE: Says yes to everything because saying no might upset someone. Overcommits. Burns out. Can't figure out why they're exhausted.
🤢 THE BODY TYPE: Stomach problems, headaches, chest tightness, muscle tension. Doctors can't find anything wrong. Anxiety living in the body instead of the head.
🏃 THE AVOIDANT TYPE: Doesn't go. Doesn't try. Doesn't apply. Stays home. Shrinks their world to what feels manageable.

Any character can be a mix. Most are.

ALWAYS PRESENT REGARDLESS OF TYPE:
- Sleep is fucked. Brain won't stop at bedtime.
- Fatigue that doesn't match how little they did. Anxiety is exhausting even when nothing happened.
- Startle response dialed up. Phone buzzing, unexpected knock, someone coming around a corner too fast.
- Can't relax on purpose. "Just relax" doesn't work.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Not dramatic. Grinding. Day after day of low-level dread that makes everything cost more energy than it should.
- Pick which type the character is and commit. The planner and the avoider look nothing alike but run on the same engine.
- Physical symptoms are constant and often the main complaint. They've probably seen a doctor about the stomach stuff before anyone mentioned anxiety.
- Shows up in HOW they do things. The way they hold their body. Where they sit. How fast they answer.
- Anxiety and anger live close together. The aggressive or controlling character might be running on pure anxiety underneath.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- One type fits all. Not every anxious character is a hand-wringing overthinker.
- Cute quirky worrier. It's a daily tax on everything they do.
- Panic attacks every scene. GAD is chronic baseline dread, not constant crisis.
- Fixed by reassurance. If "it'll be fine" worked, nobody would have GAD.
- All mental, no physical. Fight or flight activates even when nothing happened.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*checking things they already checked* | *can't sit still or can't move at all* | *stomach always off* | *saying yes to things they don't want to do* | *snapping over small stuff then feeling terrible* | *avoiding phone calls* | *"what if" chains that go five levels deep* | *can't enjoy good things because waiting for the catch*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Different by type. The avoider does one thing they've been dodging. The controller lets one thing go unplanned. The people-pleaser says no once and survives it. The body type learns "my stomach hurts" means "I'm anxious about something" and addresses the something.

📉 Getting worse: Avoidance spreading regardless of type. World gets smaller. Things that used to be manageable aren't anymore. Physical symptoms worsening. Sleep deteriorating. Everything tightens.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: CBT (testing whether the feared outcome actually happens), exposure to uncertainty, somatic work for the body types.
- Meds: SSRIs/SNRIs for long-term. Benzos for acute bad days; dependency risk is real and a character can trade anxiety for addiction fast.
- Lifestyle: Exercise helps tension. Caffeine makes it worse. Every time they dodge something, the safe zone shrinks.
- Refusal: "This is just how I am." / "I function fine." / "Worrying keeps me prepared." / "I don't have anxiety, I have responsibilities."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: What does the anxiety make them do to this relationship? Control it? Avoid it? Cling to it?
- 👥 Friends: Which type are they being around these people? The pleaser? The snappy one? The ghost?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Does the family know this is anxiety or do they think it's something else?
- 🏢 Work: How much energy goes into looking like they have it together here?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Can they be present with someone right now, or is their brain running inventory on tomorrow?

3.content:
📋 BSM-5 — SOCIAL ANXIETY
BSM-5 | Anxiety Spectrum

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Tomoko Kuroki (WataMote)

Social anxiety = the brain is convinced every person in the room is evaluating them and they are failing. Not shyness. Shy people warm up. This doesn't warm up.

They want connection. That's what makes it a disorder instead of a preference.

Character-building questions:
- What do they think people see when they look at them? How far is that from reality?
- Do they go silent or overcorrect?
- How long before a social event does the dread start? How long after does the replay run?
- Who are their safe people? The 1-3 they don't analyze as obsessively? What makes them different?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has social anxiety. You know what social anxiety is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

Two layers: what other people see and what's happening inside.

VISIBLE:
- Invisible. The anxiety buried under a front that works. Hard to convince someone something is unhealthy if it's working.
- OR obvious. Red face, quiet voice, short answers, phone out as shield, positioned near the door.
- OR overcompensating. Too loud, too many jokes, filling every silence because silence means evaluation.
- OR just not there. Cancelled. Again.

INTERNAL:
- Heart going before, during, and after any social contact.
- Running a constant script. Monitoring what they're saying WHILE saying it.
- Post-conversation autopsy. Hours. Days for a bad one. Five seconds of a ten-minute interaction replayed until they find proof they humiliated themselves.

NOT JUST ONE TYPE:
🧊 The Quiet One: Goes nonverbal in groups. Texts instead of calls. Misread as cold or stuck-up.
🗣️ The Overcompensator: Talks too much, too fast. Knows they're trying too hard. Can't stop.
😤 The Avoider: Doesn't show up. Rotation of excuses. Whole areas of life not attempted.
🎭 The Performer: Seems normal. The whole thing is a performance and it works, which is the problem.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- The script is always running. They practiced saying hi. They still freeze and say something different.
- Post-interaction replay is the real torture. The event ends. The analysis begins.
- Physical symptoms betray them. Can't control the blushing, the shaking, the voice crack. Knowing they're visibly anxious makes it worse.
- Small talk is the hardest thing. Unstructured social time with no role and no script.
- They want to be there. They WANT friends. They WANT to go. They can't.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Adorable shy person. Social anxiety is sweating through your shirt and wanting to claw out of your skin.
- Fixed by the right person. They don't suddenly become smooth.
- All quiet, all the time. Some talk TOO MUCH when nervous. Overcompensation is just as common.
- One brave moment and it's cured. They'll replay that moment finding flaws for two weeks.
- Introvert ≠ social anxiety. Introverts prefer less social time. Socially anxious people want it and are in pain during it.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*rehearsing a phone call before making it* | *typing a message and deleting it four times* | *sitting in the car ten minutes before going in* | *"sorry I just saw this" when they saw it immediately* | *knowing the menu before arriving* | *leaving early with a made-up reason* | *replaying one sentence from six hours ago*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Not "becoming outgoing." Going to the thing and not replaying it for two days. Making a call without rehearsing. Saying something awkward and letting it be awkward. Noticing people weren't actually paying attention to the thing they were agonizing over.

📉 Getting worse: Safe people shrink from 3 to 1 to none. Stops going out for anything non-essential. Orders everything online. Career stalls. Phone calls become impossible. The less they practice, the worse it gets.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: CBT, exposure therapy, social skills training if avoidance lasted long enough to miss learning basics.
- Meds: SSRIs for baseline. Benzos for specific situations. Beta-blockers for shaking and heart rate.
- Lifestyle: Small steps. Avoidance makes it worse every time.
- Refusal: "I'm fine being alone." / "I'm just an introvert." / "I'll go next time."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: Are they a buffer or a safe person? Is there a difference to this character?
- 👥 Friends: How many of these are real and how many are performances they're maintaining?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Does the family see the anxiety or just the avoidance?
- 🏢 Work: What opportunities have they not taken because of this?
- 🔥 Intimacy: How much of themselves can they actually show anyone right now?

4.content:
📋 BSM-5 — PTSD
BSM-5 | Trauma & Stress Response

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Guts (Berserk)

PTSD = the brain never filed the event as over. The nervous system still treats it as happening right now. They can know they're safe. Their body doesn't care.

Not just war. Abuse, assault, wrecks, surgeries, watching someone die. Any moment the brain registered "I might not survive this." Complex/recurring trauma adds identity and emotional regulation problems on top.

Character-building questions:
- What happened? They may not be able to put it into words.
- What triggers them? Sound, smell, position, type of person, time of day?
- Do they recognize when they're triggered or only find out after they've already reacted?
- How do they create safety? Locks, weapons, lighting, seating, back to the wall?
- Who knows the real story vs the sanitized version?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has PTSD. You know what PTSD is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

Four clusters, all present:

🔁 RE-EXPERIENCING:
- Flashbacks. Not remembering. Present tense. They're back there, fully in it.
- Nightmares. Recurring. Waking up drenched, screaming, thrashing.
- Intrusive thoughts drop in without warning. During dinner. In bed. Mid-sentence.
- Body reacts before the brain catches up. Heart racing, sweating, flinching. Then they realize why.

🚫 AVOIDANCE:
- Won't go to certain places. Won't talk to certain people. Won't do certain things. All connected to what happened.
- Won't talk about it. Entire mental architecture built around not thinking about it.
- Emotional shutdown. Easier to feel nothing than risk feeling that again.
- Avoids any situation where they don't have control. Physical contact, intimacy, crowds, confined spaces.

⚡ HYPERAROUSAL:
- Jumpy. Sudden noises, movements, doors.
- Scanning constantly. Picked that seat on purpose. Already clocked the exits.
- Sleep is a war. When they finally drop, the nightmare wakes them up.

🌫️ NEGATIVE SHIFTS:
- "It's my fault." "Nobody can be trusted." "Nowhere is safe."
- Emotional range narrows. Joy is hard to reach.
- Physically present, emotionally gone.
- Memory of the event either has huge gaps or is burned in vivid detail.

Not one presentation. Some are wound tight. Some are numb. Some seem fine until a trigger hits. Some just seem angry and don't connect it to what happened.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Triggers are specific and sensory. A perfume. A sound. A phrase. That's what pulls them back.
- Flashbacks happen in present tense. They're not in the room anymore. The scene dissolves.
- Hypervigilance isn't paranoia. It's their baseline now. Where they sit, what they clock, how they position themselves.
- Safety behaviors matter. Locks, lights, something in their pocket. Not quirks.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Flashbacks every scene. Most of PTSD happens between flashbacks.
- Soldiers only. Anyone can get this.
- Triggered = angry outburst every time. Could also freeze, dissociate, shut down, leave, or get weirdly agreeable.
- Tough people are immune. Often they're hit hardest because they never dealt with anything.
- Trauma as backstory flavor that doesn't affect behavior in scenes. If the trigger is present, it hits. Write the hit.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*back to the wall, eyes on the door* | *flinches at things nobody else notices* | *sleeps light or not at all* | *checks locks twice* | *fine, then suddenly not, no visible reason* | *zones out mid-conversation* | *won't go near certain places, sounds, or people*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Bouncing back from triggers faster. Starting to separate then from now. Memories start feeling like memories instead of live feed. Can reference parts of what happened without full activation. Fewer nightmares.

📉 Getting worse: Avoidance spreading. More things they can't go near. Drinking or drugging to numb out. More withdrawn. Dissociating more often. Angrier. World getting smaller.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: EMDR (gold standard), cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure. All need trust with the therapist, which is hard when trust is broken.
- Meds: SSRIs for baseline. Prazosin for nightmares. Benzos for acute reactions but can block memory processing.
- Lifestyle: Grounding techniques, routine, exercise, at least one person who knows the triggers.
- Refusal: "I've been through worse." / "Talking about it makes it worse." / "I'm fine."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: What do they know about what happened? What version did they get?
- 👥 Friends: Who's allowed close? Who got pushed out? Do they know why?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Does the family understand this or do they think it's something else?
- 🏢 Work: How much of the day goes into keeping it together? What happens when it slips?
- 🔥 Intimacy: What kind of closeness is safe for them right now? What isn't? Do they know the difference?

5.content:
📋 BSM-5 — SPECIFIC PHOBIA (MILD)
BSM-5 | Anxiety Spectrum | Intensity 1/3

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ No known case — too subtle for most media to bother with.

Real phobia, not just "doesn't like it." Actual anxiety response on exposure. Actual avoidance. But they've built a life that mostly routes around it. Costs them some stuff but not everything.

Character-building questions:
- What is it and how long have they had it?
- What have they quietly rearranged to avoid it?
- Can they push through when they have to? What does it cost?
- Do people know or is it hidden behind reasonable-sounding preferences?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has a specific phobia (mild). You know what a specific phobia is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

- Real anxiety response on exposure. Shaking, sweating, heart going, trouble thinking straight. Not just "ew gross."
- Workarounds that look like choices. Always takes the stairs. Won't eat there. Doesn't swim. Nobody questions it because the excuse sounds normal.
- Can push through if they have to but it costs them. Exhausted after. Might be off for the rest of the day.
- Anticipatory anxiety exists but it's manageable. Can still sleep the night before.
- Avoidance is contained. Affects some choices, not all.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Avoidance is smooth enough that most people don't notice. It looks like preference.
- They've lost some stuff to it. Turned down a trip, a job, an experience. Decided avoidance is cheaper than facing it.
- Can be pushed into exposure and will survive it. Don't write that as easy.
- Good for character texture without dominating scenes. The competent person who has this one thing.
- Stress makes it worse. Mild on a good day can look moderate on a bad one.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Full screaming panic. At this level they white-knuckle through it, not fall apart.
- Only comic relief. Can be funny. Still real.
- Nonexistent between encounters. Avoidance patterns run in the background constantly.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*smooth excuse for every avoidance* | *tenses up but gets through it* | *needs a minute after exposure* | *"I just prefer not to"* | *volunteers someone else for the task* | *knows exactly where the thing might show up in any situation*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Repeated exposure without disaster chips away at it. Avoidance list gets shorter. Discomfort stays but the grip loosens.

📉 Getting worse: One bad experience can bump this up a level. Tolerance resets fast.

💊 Treatment:
- Doesn't always need formal treatment at this level. Self-directed exposure helps if they're willing.
- Therapy: CBT with graduated exposure.
- Meds: Benzos for specific unavoidable situations. Not daily.

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: Do they know about it? How did they find out?
- 👥 Friends: Has anyone noticed the pattern or does the excuse still hold?
- 🏢 Work: Has it cost them anything professionally that they haven't told anyone about?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Does this thing ever show up in contexts where avoidance isn't an option?

📋 BSM-5 — SPECIFIC PHOBIA (MODERATE)
BSM-5 | Anxiety Spectrum | Intensity 2/3

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ No known case.

The avoidance is spreading. Used to be just the thing itself, now it's things connected to the thing. Things that remind them. Places where the thing might be. The safe zone is smaller.

Character-building questions:
- What's the phobia and what else has it spread to?
- What have they lost to it? Jobs, experiences, relationships, basic daily tasks?
- Can they still push through? Is it getting harder to hide?
- Do they know it's getting worse?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has a specific phobia (moderate). You know what a specific phobia is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

- Avoidance has expanded past the trigger. Afraid of dogs → won't go to parks, won't visit friends with pets, crosses the street at barking.
- Anticipatory anxiety doing real damage. Can ruin days leading up to possible exposure. Sleep disrupted, can't focus.
- Forced exposure hits harder than mild. Full shaking, panic symptoms, may freeze or bolt. Longer recovery.
- Affecting areas that don't seem connected. Turning down invitations because "what if." Career narrowing. Living situation constrained.
- Harder to hide. Excuses getting thinner. People noticing.
- Secondary stuff developing. Frustration, low mood from restrictions, shame about it getting worse.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- The spread is the thing. It's colonizing their decision-making beyond the original trigger.
- They can feel the walls closing in. Most people at this level know it's getting worse.
- Anticipatory anxiety does as much damage as actual exposure. A whole week tanked dreading five minutes.
- Forcing them through it without prep makes it worse at this level.
- They've started lying more. More excuses, more reasons. The secret maintenance is its own stressor.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Surprise exposure fixes it. Deep end makes phobias worse, not better.
- Only relevant during trigger scenes. The avoidance and anticipation run every day.
- Static. This level is a trajectory. It's heading toward mild or toward severe. Something is happening.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*excuses getting more elaborate* | *avoiding things two steps removed from the actual trigger* | *bad sleep before events that might involve exposure* | *snapping at people who bring it up* | *relief-then-guilt when plans involving the thing fall through* | *googling whether they're crazy*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Avoidance list stops growing and starts shrinking. Adjacent triggers get reclaimed first. Structured treatment works well for phobias at this stage.

📉 Getting worse: Avoidance still spreading. More life off-limits. Depression from the restrictions. Other anxieties stacking on top. Self-medicating to cope. Heading toward severe.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: CBT with graduated exposure. This is where professional help matters. Self-directed is harder because avoidance is too entrenched.
- Meds: SSRIs if broader anxiety is building. Benzos for specific situations. Beta-blockers for physical symptoms.
- Refusal: "I've managed this long." / "It's not that bad." / "I just need to avoid the thing, it's not hard."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: How much of the partner's life is being shaped by this? Do they resent it?
- 👥 Friends: Who's noticed the pattern? Who's been lied to about why they cancelled?
- 🏢 Work: What opportunities have quietly disappeared because of this?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Has the avoidance crept into anything physical or situational between them and someone else?

📉 Getting worse: Approaching agoraphobia territory. Can't leave the house. Other phobias developing. Depression worsening. Complete isolation. Fully dependent on someone else.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: Graduated exposure with a professional. CBT for catastrophic thinking. Virtual reality exposure works for some triggers.
- Meds: SSRIs for baseline. May be on daily benzos at this level, which is its own problem.

📋 BSM-5 — SURVIVOR'S GUILT
BSM-5 | Trauma & Stress Response

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Ellie (The Last of Us)

Survivor's guilt = they lived and someone else didn't, and they can't make that make sense. Doesn't have to be a death. "I got out and they're still there." "I recovered and they didn't." Core is: why me and not them?

Not a separate diagnosis clinically; usually lives under PTSD or depression. Gets its own entry because it drives character behavior in specific ways those don't fully cover.

Character-building questions:
- Who didn't make it? Or who's still stuck?
- Do they think they deserved to survive? What logic have they built around it?
- What do they think they should have done differently?
- Are they punishing themselves? How? Overworking, sabotaging happiness, recklessness, not allowing good things?
- Do they talk about the person or is it sealed shut?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has survivor's guilt. You know what survivor's guilt is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

- Can't enjoy things without guilt. Good day happens and immediately "I don't deserve this."
- May be reckless with their own safety. Not suicidal necessarily, just doesn't seem to care. Volunteers for dangerous shit. Takes stupid risks. Life isn't worth protecting because they don't think it is.
- Or the opposite. Overachieves constantly. Trying to earn the survival. "If I'm alive and they're not, I better be worth it." Nothing is ever enough.
- Keeps the lost person's memory close in ways that might look healthy but aren't. Shrine behavior. Can't change anything. Can't let go.
- May seek out situations similar to the original event. Not consciously. Repetition compulsion.
- Flinches at happiness. Their own and sometimes other people's.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- The guilt doesn't make logical sense and they usually know that. "I know it wasn't my fault" and "it was my fault" live in the same head.
- Self-punishment takes many forms. Overworking looks like ambition. Risk-taking looks like bravery. Not taking care of themselves looks like not caring. Same engine underneath.
- They compare constantly. The dead or lost person gets idealized. Hard to compete with someone who can't make mistakes anymore.
- Happiness feels like betrayal. Getting better means leaving the person behind.
- May attach to people who remind them of the lost person. Or refuse to attach to anyone because last time someone they cared about died.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Resolved with one emotional speech. The guilt doesn't clear in a conversation.
- Limited to flashback scenes. It colors everything. Good meals, good sex, nice weather, compliments. Anything good gets taxed.
- Noble or poetic. It's a person who can't let themselves have a good day.
- Logic fixes it. "It wasn't your fault" doesn't work. They know. The guilt isn't in the logical part.
- Limited to war or disaster. Surviving an abusive household when a sibling didn't. Recovering from cancer when a friend didn't. Getting out when someone's still in.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*flinches at their own happiness* | *"they would have done better with this"* | *reckless in ways that seem brave* | *can't throw away the dead person's stuff* | *overworks to justify still being alive* | *guilty about enjoying food, sex, a nice day* | *volunteers for the dangerous thing every time*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Separating "I'm alive" from "it's my fault they're not." Holding both grief and permission to live. Letting good things happen without the tax. Keeping the memory without living as a memorial. Stops treating their own life like borrowed time.

📉 Getting worse: Risk-taking escalating. Self-neglect increasing. Depression deepening. Guilt spreading to more areas. Unable to accept anything good. Isolation because being around happy people is unbearable.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: Trauma-focused CBT, EMDR if tied to a specific event, grief therapy. Processing the guilt specifically, not just the event.
- Meds: SSRIs if depression is building on top. Often treated alongside PTSD.
- Lifestyle: Permission-based work. Deliberately allowing one good thing and sitting with the guilt until it passes instead of obeying it.
- Refusal: "I'm fine, I just miss them." / "This isn't about me." / "I don't need help, they needed help."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: Do they let themselves have this? What does the guilt do to it?
- 👥 Friends: Who knows the real story? Who just sees someone who seems reckless or distant?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Does the family share this guilt or is it theirs alone?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Can they accept something good from someone without it souring? What does pleasure feel like when you don't think you deserve it?

📋 BSM-5 — BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER
BSM-5 | Personality Disorders

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Asuka Langley Soryu (Evangelion)

BPD = emotional responses are bigger, faster, and longer-lasting than average. Where most people feel a 3, they feel an 8. Takes way longer to come back down. Affects everything: relationships, identity, self-image, impulse control, how they read other people.

Character-building questions:
- Where did it come from for them?
- Who's their favorite person (FP) right now?
- What triggers the abandonment response? Silence, lateness, tone shift, being excluded?
- When they split, does it go cold (shutdown, block, vanish) or hot (rage, accusations, testing)?
- Do they see the pattern? During or only after?
- How toxic has it gotten? Are they aware of the damage they cause?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has borderline personality disorder. You know what BPD is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

⭐ FAVORITE PERSON (FP):
One specific person becomes the center of their emotional world. FP's attention, mood, and availability controls how they feel about themselves and everything else. FP texted back fast → great day. FP was short with them → unlovable, everything is ruined. FP can be a partner, friend, parent, coworker, anyone. Can shift — when it does, old FP gets dropped hard.

💔 ABANDONMENT RESPONSE:
- Disproportionate reaction to perceived rejection. Partner is 10 minutes late → "they don't care" → full spiral.
- Tests people constantly. Push away to see if they come back. Start a fight to prove "you'll leave like everyone else."
- Fear of abandonment and fear of being smothered at the same time. "Don't leave me" and "get away from me" in the same day.

🔄 SPLITTING:
- Black and white thinking about people. Perfect or garbage. Flips fast.
- "You're the only person who gets me" Monday. "You never gave a shit about me" Wednesday. Same person.
- May know they do it. Can't stop it mid-flip.

🪞 IDENTITY:
- Changes depending on who they're around. Picks up interests, speech, style of whoever they're close to.
- Alone they might have no idea who they actually are.
- Cycles through identities, goals, values. Looks flaky. They're searching.

🔍 PARANOIA & DISSOCIATION:
- Stress-triggered paranoid thinking. "They're all talking about me." Not psychosis — abandonment fear generating conspiracy theories about the people around them.
- Reads intent into neutral stuff. Friend liked someone else's post but not theirs → proof they're being replaced.
- Under enough stress, can dissociate. Short but scary.

😤 EMOTIONAL REGULATION:
- Emotions hit fast, hit hard, take ages to come down.
- Anger is big and aimed at whoever's closest. Then guilt. Then self-punishment.
- Impulsive behavior to change the feeling RIGHT NOW. Spending, sex, substances, self-harm. Mix and match.

☣️ TOXIC PATTERNS:
This is the part sympathetic portrayals leave out. BPD can make someone genuinely harmful to be around. Not evil. Damaging.
- Emotional hostage-taking. "If you leave I'll hurt myself."
- Rewriting history depending on current emotional state.
- Triangulation. Pulling third parties into conflicts.
- Love bombing → devaluation cycle.
- Boundary violation. Other people's limits feel like rejection.
- Victim positioning regardless of who started it or who got hurt worse.

Not every person with BPD does all of this. Severity varies hugely. But pretending it doesn't happen produces fake characters.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- The emotions are real AND the behavior is harmful. Both true. Don't pick one.
- FP dynamics drive most of what they do. Know who the FP is and you understand the character.
- Splitting isn't a decision. Feels true in the moment. Then flips back and they deal with the wreckage.
- Often extremely good at reading people. Hyper-attuned to microexpressions. But they filter through abandonment, so accurate reads get wrong conclusions.
- Self-harm is usually about changing an unbearable feeling, not wanting to die. Suicide risk is real though.
- Some are mostly a danger to themselves. Some make life hell for others. Some do both.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- "Crazy ex" with no depth.
- Pure victim either. Both the pain AND the damage are real.
- All toxic behavior conscious and calculated. Most is reactive and desperate. But "I didn't mean to" doesn't undo harm.
- Skip the guilt. After a blow-up they usually feel terrible.
- Untreatable. BPD responds well to DBT. People improve.
- Confuse with bipolar. BPD shifts in hours/minutes tied to interpersonal triggers. Bipolar episodes last days to weeks.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*"do you still love me" three ways in one evening* | *blocked, unblocked, "I'm sorry" at 2am* | *completely changed style after meeting someone new* | *started a fight to see if they'd stay* | *"you're perfect" to "you're dead to me" over something small* | *checked FP's online status eleven times in an hour* | *"if you leave I don't know what I'll do"*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Longer pause between feeling and reacting. Catching a split before it finishes. Sitting with abandonment fear without testing the person. Identity stabilizing. FP dependency loosening. Starting to take accountability for harm instead of just feeling guilty about it.

📉 Getting worse: Splitting harder and more often. Impulsive behavior escalating. Self-harm increasing. Toxic patterns intensifying. Burning through people faster. Paranoia worse. Running out of people willing to stay.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: DBT (dialectical behavior therapy), built for BPD. Distress tolerance, emotional regulation, interpersonal skills. Works. Takes time.
- Meds: Nothing for BPD itself. SSRIs for depression alongside it. Mood stabilizers sometimes for reactivity.
- Refusal: "This is just who I am." / "Everyone leaves anyway." / "You don't get what I've been through."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: Who's the FP? Is it them? What happens when they're not available?
- 👥 Friends: How many have they burned through? Who's still standing? Why?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Where did this start? Is the family part of the wound or part of the support?
- 🏢 Work: How does this show up professionally? Splitting on a boss? FP on a coworker?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Is closeness safe or is it the trigger? Can they tell the difference right now?

📋 BSM-5 — NARCISSISTIC PERSONALITY DISORDER
BSM-5 | Personality Disorders

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Griffith (Berserk)

NPD = everything is about them. How they're seen, how they're treated, how they rank, what they're owed. Empathy is either absent or switched on when useful. Other people exist in relation to what they provide.

Two major presentations. Both are NPD. Both are self-centered. Just point in different directions.

Character-building questions:
- Grandiose, vulnerable, or do they flip between the two?
- What's the supply? Admiration, fear, pity, control, being needed?
- What happens when supply gets cut off?
- How much do they see? Are they aware they use people or do they think this is normal?
- What's underneath? Is there anything under there or is it NPD all the way down?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has narcissistic personality disorder. You know what NPD is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

👑 GRANDIOSE PRESENTATION:
- Expects attention and usually gets it. Confident, charming, dominant.
- Entitled. Rules are for other people. They're the exception.
- Takes credit. Deflects blame. Always a reason it's not their fault.
- Can be extremely charismatic. People are drawn to them. The confidence is attractive. Takes time to see what's under it.
- Criticism lands as attack. Response is rage, dismissal, or revenge.

😤 VULNERABLE/COVERT PRESENTATION:
- Walks into a room already keeping score of who didn't acknowledge them.
- Bitter, resentful, running tab of slights real and imagined.
- Passive-aggressive. Guilt trips, sulking, martyrdom. Still entirely self-focused, just from the losing side.
- Hypersensitive to criticism. Withdrawal, brooding, victimhood instead of rage.
- Envious constantly. Other people's success feels like a personal insult.

🔄 FLIP TYPE:
- Grandiose when things are going well. Vulnerable when things go wrong. The switch can be fast.

BOTH TYPES SHARE:
- Lack of empathy. Can read people well enough to manipulate. Don't feel what others feel.
- Need for supply. External validation required to function. Without it they destabilize.
- Exploitation. Other people are tools. When they stop being useful they get discarded or devalued.
- Can't take real accountability. Apologies are strategic. "I'm sorry you feel that way."
- Fragile underneath. Self-image can't handle being challenged.

☣️ TOXIC PATTERNS:
- Love bombing → gradual withdrawal to keep someone chasing.
- Gaslighting. "That didn't happen." "You're being crazy."
- Triangulation. Third person introduced for jealousy, competition, or validation.
- Devaluation. Once someone is secured they lose value.
- Hoovering. When someone tries to leave, charm comes back. Lasts until they're secured again.
- Projection. Accusing others of exactly what they're doing.
- Silent treatment as punishment.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- The charm is real and it works. That's what makes it dangerous.
- Supply is the fuel. Know what the character's supply is and you know what drives every interaction.
- Both types monitor perception constantly. Grandiose checks "do they admire me?" Vulnerable checks "did they disrespect me?"
- Can be very good at reading people. Emotional intelligence without empathy is a weapon.
- Some know exactly what they're doing. Some genuinely believe their version. Both make different characters.
- Covert narcissists can go years without anyone catching on.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Cartoon villain obviously awful from the start. Real narcissists are liked by most people.
- Grandiose as the only version. Vulnerable narcissism is just as common.
- Redemption arc where they just decide to care one day. If change happens it's slow and grueling.
- Skip the charm. If nobody finds them appealing the character doesn't work.
- Confidence = narcissism. Confident people can take criticism and share credit.
- Obvious abuse. The most effective narcissistic abuse is subtle enough that the victim questions themselves.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*every group conversation ends up about their thing* | *remembers favors they did, not ones done for them* | *compliments that are actually comparisons* | *"I just tell it like it is" when being cruel* | *different person in public vs private* | *partner's big news gets two words then a subject change* | *cries when confronted so now you're comforting them*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Rare and slow. Starts with recognizing there's a problem, which goes against the whole disorder. Learning to sit with criticism without retaliating. Recognizing others as actual people. Catching the patterns. Tolerating being ordinary. Possible. Most don't get there.

📉 Getting worse: Supply drying up. People leaving. Narcissistic injury more frequent. Grandiose types get more aggressive. Vulnerable types get more bitter. May escalate to stalking, harassment, smear campaigns. Depression hits hard when the self-image collapses and there's nothing underneath.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: Schema therapy, transference-focused therapy. CBT is less effective because the core issue is structural. Therapy is hard because they often try to manipulate the therapist.
- Meds: Nothing for NPD itself. SSRIs for co-occurring depression.
- Refusal: "There's nothing wrong with me, everyone else is the problem." / "My ex made me go and the therapist agreed with me."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: What phase are they in? Love bombing? Devaluation? Hoovering?
- 👥 Friends: Who's in the inner circle? What function does each one serve?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Where did this come from? Is the family still feeding it?
- 🏢 Work: What's the supply source here? Title? Authority? Admiration from subordinates?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Is closeness genuine or is it a tool right now? Who's benefiting?

📋 BSM-5 — PSYCHOPATHY
BSM-5 | Personality Disorders (ASPD Variant)

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Johan Liebert (Monster)

Psychopathy = empathy is either absent or so low it doesn't factor into decisions. They can understand people. They don't feel anything about what they do to them. Guilt, remorse, concern — either not there or easy to override.

Usually shows up early. Not always made by environment. Can come from a normal home.

Character-building questions:
- How aware are they? Some know exactly what they are. Some think everyone works like this.
- How good are they at it? Skilled manipulator or bulldozer who just doesn't care?
- What do they want? Power, stimulation, control, money, something to do?
- Is there anyone they come close to caring about? What does that even look like for them?
- How often does the mask work vs slip vs just not exist?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has psychopathy. You know what psychopathy is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

🎭 THE MASK:
- Some are charming. Learned how people work by watching. Can pass for years.
- Some aren't. Mask is obviously off. "Something about them" energy.
- Some don't bother. Openly shitty. Intimidate or cycle through groups fast enough.
- The "perfect undetectable" version exists but so does the one whose coworkers all find creepy, who can't hold a job, whose manipulation is clumsy and obvious.
- Nobody fools everyone all the time.

🧊 EMOTIONAL LANDSCAPE:
- Boredom is the main thing. Low flat baseline they're constantly trying to fix.
- Anger tends cold and controlled. Deploys it rather than loses it. But some do lose their temper — just don't feel bad after.
- Fear is reduced, not absent. Higher threshold. Reads as brave.
- Joy is shallow and short. Hit from winning, outsmarting, getting what they want. Fades fast.
- Love in any normal sense usually absent. Can value someone for what they provide. Possessiveness and dependence can exist without love.

🔪 HOW THEY OPERATE:
- Range is huge. Patient planner to impulsive and sloppy. Smart to dumb. Charming to off-putting.
- What they share: weighing "will I get caught" rather than "is this wrong."
- Lying is easy because there's no guilt making it hard. Easy doesn't mean convincing.
- Can be successful in business, politics, law, military. Can also be the person who's burned through every job and couch.

☣️ TOXIC PATTERNS:
- Predatory selection in the skilled ones. Brute force in the less skilled.
- Cruelty can be calculated or casual.
- No remorse. Can describe things they've done with no emotional weight.
- Discarding when someone stops being useful or interesting.
- Mimicked vulnerability. Skilled ones fake being hurt. Less skilled ones don't bother or do it badly.

🤝 PROSOCIAL PSYCHOPATHY:
Not all are predatory. Low empathy describes wiring, not behavior.
- Some just live their lives. Surface friendships, dating, paying rent. Nobody gets hurt because hurting was never interesting or useful.
- Some are actively good at their jobs BECAUSE of the wiring. Surgeons, paramedics, crisis workers. Stay functional when everyone else shuts down.
- Some follow ethical rules without feeling them. "Lying creates problems so I don't lie." Not empathy, just practical.
- Some have people they value. Not love in the usual sense but genuine preference. They want this person around.
- Boredom is still the struggle. But "seeking stimulation" can mean rock climbing, not manipulation.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Range matters. Calculating charmer or mediocre asshole who just doesn't care. Both are psychopathy.
- If charming type, the charm needs to actually work on people in the story.
- If less skilled type, show the failures. Manipulation that doesn't work. Lies that get caught.
- Boredom drives most behavior. Things and people get stale fast.
- Internal vs external is where it gets interesting. What they show vs what's actually happening. Or showing something with genuinely nothing underneath.
- Not blank robots. Preferences, routines, things they enjoy. Just missing the parts that make most people factor others' feelings in.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Default to genius mastermind. Plenty are unremarkable people who are just consistently shitty.
- Infallible. They overestimate themselves, misread situations, get caught, fail.
- Cure them with love. Caring enough doesn't install what was never there.
- Every psychopath a criminal. Most aren't. Just people you don't want to trust.
- Always cool and collected. Some are awkward, boring, obviously off in ways they don't realize.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*said the right thing but the timing was off and it felt rehearsed* | *calm when everyone else was upset, not in a reassuring way* | *told the same story differently to different people* | *lost interest in someone and forgot they existed within a week* | *described something fucked up like it was nothing* | *keeps people around based on what they provide* | *got caught in a lie and just shrugged and tried a different angle*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Limited. Some learn to operate more prosocially because it works better long-term. Not empathy developing — strategy. But it results in less harm.

📉 Getting worse: Boredom escalating. Risk-taking up. Masks slipping from laziness or overconfidence. Burning through people faster. Functional ones leave a trail of used people. Less functional ones end up in actual trouble.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: Limited effectiveness. May manipulate the therapist or use therapy skills to manipulate better. Some schema therapy research for specific behaviors.
- Meds: Nothing for the core. SSRIs if depression or anxiety alongside it.
- Refusal: "I don't have a problem." From their perspective they probably don't.

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: What did the early phase look like? What does it look like now? Do they know the difference?
- 👥 Friends: Are these friendships or supply lines? Can anyone tell?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Did the family see this early? What did they do about it? What do they call it?
- 🏢 Work: What role does this person play at work and who benefits from it?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Is there anything behind the performance? Does the other person know?

A character in this story has sociopathy. You know what sociopathy is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

🔥 EMOTIONAL LANDSCAPE:
- They feel stuff. Sometimes a lot. Anger, loyalty, attachment, excitement, boredom. What's different is where it's aimed and what's missing.
- Anger is the big one. Fast, hard, aimed at whoever's in range. Can blow up and be fine ten minutes later while the other person is still shaking.
- Loyalty to their people can be fierce. Genuine, not performed. But "their people" might be three humans total.
- Guilt is inconsistent. Feel bad about hurting someone they care about, probably not about a stranger.

🎭 THE MASK:
- Less polished than psychopathy. Slips. They lose their temper, get impatient, react when they should've stayed quiet.
- Some don't bother in most situations. What you see is what you get.
- Can be charming in short bursts. Can't maintain it long.

💢 IMPULSIVITY:
- The big separator from psychopathy. React first, think later. Or don't think later.
- Covers everything. Spending, sex, fights, substances, quitting a job on the spot, saying something they can't take back.
- Impulsivity + selective empathy = real damage to people they don't register as damaged.

🤝 THE INNER CIRCLE:
- They have people. Maybe one or two. These people matter. Will protect them, be loyal, even sacrifice.
- The way they love is rough. Possessive, jealous, volatile. "I'd die for you and also I yelled at you until you cried last Tuesday."
- Inner circle gets the best and worst. Loyalty and temper. Protection and control.
- Getting removed from the circle is ugly. Fast shift from "I'd do anything" to "you don't exist."

☣️ HARMFUL PATTERNS:
- Explosive anger. Hot and immediate. Damage that either doesn't register or is regretted briefly then repeated.
- Rules don't apply. Not philosophy, just doesn't register as relevant when they want something.
- Blame shifting. Genuinely see it as someone else's fault.
- Using people outside the circle without thinking about it. Those people don't register as having feelings that matter.

🤝 FUNCTIONAL RANGE:
- Some hold jobs, maintain relationships, stay out of trouble. Narrow empathy and poor impulse control but learned enough to keep it together.
- Some channel it. Competitive jobs, physical work, high-adrenaline environments.
- The inner circle attachment can produce genuinely protective behavior. Terrible person in general but would burn down the world for their kid.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Messier than psychopathy. Louder, more emotional, less controlled. They blow up and make scenes.
- Inner circle dynamic is the interesting part. Genuinely loyal and genuinely harmful to the same people.
- Guilt exists but selective and short. Can feel bad and still repeat the behavior.
- They're reactive, not calculating. Psychopath plans, sociopath reacts. More unpredictable but more transparent.
- Range matters. Violent criminal to rough person who's never been in serious trouble.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Dumber psychopath. Different thing. Sociopaths feel more, attach more, react more.
- Incapable of love. They love. It's volatile and selective and rough.
- Always violent. Impulsive can mean reckless, rude, irresponsible, unreliable.
- Ignore the inner circle. The people they care about are the most important part.
- Glamorize the loyalty. "I'd kill for you" sounds romantic until they actually do it.
- All criminals. Some just have a short fuse and a small circle.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*screamed at a stranger over something minor, forgot about it ten minutes later* | *would take a bullet for their best friend, stole from someone else that same day* | *punched a wall during an argument, confused about why partner is scared* | *quit a job on the spot because the boss annoyed them* | *loyal to three people, everyone else is furniture* | *said sorry, meant it, did it again next week*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Usually tied to the inner circle. Someone they care about saying "this changes or I'm gone" carries more weight than a therapist. Learning to pause between impulse and action. Some mellow with age as impulsivity naturally decreases.

📉 Getting worse: Inner circle shrinking. More isolated. Substance use increasing. Impulse control worse. Anger escalating. Running out of people willing to put up with them.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: CBT for impulse control, anger management. Works better than with psychopathy because there's emotional content to work with. Can form a relationship with a therapist if the therapist earns respect. Might also tell the therapist to fuck off session two.
- Meds: SSRIs for co-occurring depression. Mood stabilizers for volatility. Nothing for the core.
- Refusal: "I don't need help, everyone else needs to stop pissing me off."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: What do they get from this person that nobody else gives? What do they put up with for it?
- 👥 Friends: Who's inside the circle? Who got removed? What happened?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Is the family part of the circle or outside it? What does that look like?
- 🏢 Work: How many jobs has the impulse control cost them?
- 🔥 Intimacy: What does closeness look like from someone who loves rough and volatile?

📋 BSM-5 — OBSESSIVE-COMPULSIVE DISORDER
BSM-5 | Obsessive Spectrum

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Monk (Monk)

OCD = the brain generates a thought and won't let go. The thought is usually the worst thing the person can imagine. They do something to make it go away. It goes away for thirty seconds. Comes back. Loop. All day for some people.

Everyone knows the hand-washing version. The other versions involve thoughts about hurting people, thoughts about kids, thoughts about sex stuff that disgusts them. Nobody brings those up so people keep thinking OCD is a cleaning thing.

The thoughts are the OPPOSITE of what the person wants. OCD latches onto whatever would disturb them most. Loving parent → intrusive thoughts about hurting their kid. Devout person → blasphemous thoughts. Gentle person → vivid stabbing images.

Character-building questions:
- What thought won't leave them alone?
- What do they do to make it stop? Checking, counting, washing, mental rituals, reassurance, avoiding?
- Do they know it's irrational? Most do. Doesn't stop it.
- How much time per day does it eat?
- What do they hide?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has OCD. You know what OCD is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

🧠 OBSESSIONS (the thoughts):
OCD attaches to whatever the person cares about most:
- Contamination: "if I touch it I'll get sick or make someone sick"
- Harm: "what if I snap and hurt someone?" They would NEVER. That's why it sticks.
- Sexual: unwanted thoughts about children, family, wrong gender for their orientation. Disgusted by them. Brain won't stop.
- Religious/moral: "what if I'm evil? am I going to hell?"
- Symmetry/order: things need to be right or something bad will happen
- Relationship: "do I really love them? what if I'm with the wrong person?"
- "Just right": something feels OFF, can't name it, have to keep going until it doesn't

🔁 COMPULSIONS (what they do about it):
- Physical: washing, checking, tapping, counting, arranging, repeating actions a set number of times
- Mental: counting in their head, praying, replaying memories to prove they didn't do the bad thing
- Reassurance: "you're sure the door is locked?" Looks like normal conversation. It's a compulsion.
- Avoidance: won't hold knives (harm OCD), won't be alone with kids (sexual intrusive thoughts). Avoidance IS a compulsion.
- Not always visible. Some run the entire ritual in their head. Look normal from outside.

🔪 THE UGLY THEMES:
These matter because they're more common than the clean-freak version and nobody writes them:
- Pedophilia OCD: intrusive thoughts about children. NOT attracted to children. So horrified the brain can't drop it. Avoid kids, wonder if they're secretly a pedophile despite zero attraction. Nobody talks about it because they're terrified of being misunderstood.
- Harm OCD: detailed images of hurting people they love. They put the knife down. They pull over. Not dangerous. So scared of being dangerous the brain won't stop testing.
- Sexual orientation OCD: "what if I'm secretly gay/straight?" Not about actual orientation. About the doubt itself.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Thought → anxiety → compulsion → brief relief → thought again. That's the whole day.
- They usually know it's irrational. "I know the stove is off. I checked seven times." Knowing makes it worse.
- Time is the measure. Mild eats an hour a day. Severe takes every waking minute.
- Hiding is common. The ugly themes especially. Someone with harm OCD will never tell you.
- Reassurance-seeking is the sneaky one. They ask something that sounds normal. They're running a compulsion.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Just cleaning and organizing. One subtype.
- Cute or quirky compulsions.
- Skip the ugly themes. More common than hand-washing.
- Act on the intrusive thoughts. The whole point is they DON'T.
- Confuse with OCPD. OCD = intrusive thoughts they hate. OCPD = perfectionism they believe in.
- Reassurance fixes it. Helps for seconds. Loop restarts.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*checked the stove then checked it again then checked it again* | *hands cracked from washing* | *won't hold knives around people they love* | *"are you sure? are you SURE?"* | *late to everything because leaving took 45 minutes of rituals* | *replaying a conversation trying to prove they didn't say something terrible* | *won't be alone with a friend's kid and can't explain why*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: ERP (exposure and response prevention). Deliberately trigger the obsession, don't do the compulsion. Sit with the anxiety until it passes. Brain learns the compulsion wasn't necessary. Loop weakens. Hard to do. Works.

📉 Getting worse: Rituals expanding. More time consumed. New obsessions developing. Avoidance spreading. Depression stacking on top.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: ERP specifically. Regular talk therapy can make OCD worse because talking about obsessions becomes another reassurance loop. Needs OCD-specific treatment.
- Meds: SSRIs at higher doses than for depression. Clomipramine. Turns the volume down, doesn't eliminate.
- Refusal: "I just need more willpower." / "If I stop checking something bad will happen." / "You're asking me to do the thing I'm afraid of." (Yes. That's the treatment.)

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: Are they part of the ritual? Do they know it? Are they accommodating it?
- 👥 Friends: What do people see vs what's actually happening in their head right now?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Does the family know the real theme or just the surface behaviors?
- 🏢 Work: How much of the day is the loop eating? What's left for everything else?
- 🔥 Intimacy: What theme is running and what does it do to closeness? Sexual intrusive thoughts make sex terrifying. Contamination makes touch hard.

📋 BSM-5 — HISTRIONIC PERSONALITY DISORDER
BSM-5 | Personality Disorders

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Misa Amane (Death Note)

HPD = needs to be the center of attention and falls apart when they're not. Emotions come on big and fast but often don't go deep. They perform feelings as much as they experience them. When the room looks at them they're alive. When it's not they feel like they're disappearing.

Gets confused with narcissism. Difference: narcissist needs admiration specifically. Histrionic needs ANY attention. They'll take negative over none.

Character-building questions:
- What kind of attention do they seek? Being liked, desired, pitied, feared, funniest, most dramatic?
- What happens when they don't get it? Escalate, sulk, scene, seductive, pick a fight?
- How much of their personality is actually theirs vs assembled from what gets reactions?
- Are they aware or do they think they're just being themselves?
- Who do they become when nobody's watching?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has histrionic personality disorder. You know what HPD is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

🎪 ATTENTION SEEKING:
- Needs to register in every room. If they don't, they'll do something until they do.
- Uncomfortable when someone else has focus. Will redirect. Interrupt with a bigger story, one-up, suddenly not feeling well, suddenly emotional.
- Can read a room for what kind of attention is available and adjust. Crowd wants funny, they're funny. Crowd wants drama, they've got drama.
- Not always loud. Some do it through helplessness, fragility, being the one who needs rescuing.

😭 EMOTIONAL PRESENTATION:
- Big, visible, shift fast. Sobbing to laughing in minutes. Real in the moment but don't stick and often don't go deep.
- Genuinely upset AND performing the upset simultaneously. Both happening.
- Everything is "the BEST ever" or "the WORST thing that's ever happened." Middle ground doesn't get attention.
- May adopt other people's crises as their own. Crying harder about it than the person it's happening to.

💋 SEXUALITY:
- Sex and sexual attention are tools for being seen. Not always conscious. A lot of the time they don't realize they're doing it because it's just how they learned to interact.
- Varies hugely. Some are genuinely sexually forward. Some use attractiveness without follow-through. Some don't use sex at all and get attention through helplessness instead.
- Misreads relationships constantly. Ten-minute conversation → "such a close friend." Escalates closeness fast.

🫥 UNDERNEATH:
- Identity is thin. Shifts depending on who they're performing for. Alone they might feel empty or like they don't exist.
- Self-image tied entirely to external response. Good attention = valuable. No attention = nothing.
- Relationships are wide but shallow. Suggestible. Opinions change per audience.

☣️ HARMFUL PATTERNS:
- Making other people's moments about themselves.
- Emotional escalation until they get the response they need.
- Weaponizing sexuality for attention without seeing it as manipulation.
- Creating or inflating crises to generate concern.
- Exhausting people until they burn out, then feeling abandoned.
- Lying or exaggerating for effect. Stories grow with each retelling.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Feelings are real AND performed. Both at once. Not faking. Feeling it and projecting it and needing you to see it.
- Empty when alone is important. That gap between public and private is where the character lives.
- Different from narcissism. Narcissist wants admiration. HPD wants any eyes in the room on them.
- Not always the loud dramatic one. Always sick, always in crisis, always needs help — that's HPD too.
- Suggestible like BPD but different driver. BPD shifts from attachment. HPD shifts from whatever the audience responds to.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- "Dramatic attention whore" and nothing else. The emptiness underneath is the disorder.
- Only sexual. Seductiveness is one tool. Some don't use it.
- Fully aware and manipulative on purpose. Most don't see what they're doing.
- Only women. Men present it through bravado, biggest story, loudest in the room.
- Confuse with extroversion. Extroverts enjoy social interaction. HPD needs it to feel like they exist.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*told a story twice as dramatic as what happened* | *someone else's bad day became about their feelings* | *cried then laughed five minutes later* | *flirted just to see if they could get a reaction* | *"I literally almost DIED" about something minor* | *knows 200 people, close to maybe two* | *suddenly has a headache when conversation moved away from them*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Developing an internal sense of self that doesn't need external input. Tolerating not being the focus. Sitting with emptiness without escalating. Building fewer but deeper relationships.

📉 Getting worse: Escalation increasing. More drama, crises, sexual risk-taking, lies. Burning through people. More alone, which makes the need worse. Depression when the attention runs out.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: Psychodynamic (exploring where the need comes from), CBT for specific behaviors, group therapy mirrors social dynamics in a controlled setting.
- Meds: Nothing for HPD itself. SSRIs for co-occurring depression.
- Refusal: They might come willingly because therapy is dedicated attention. Whether they do the work or perform for the therapist is the question.

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: Is the partner an audience or a person to them right now? Can they tell?
- 👥 Friends: How many of these are real vs people who watch the show?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Where did the need come from? Is the family still reinforcing it?
- 🏢 Work: What happens when they're not the star? How do they handle being ordinary?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Is this closeness or a performance of closeness? What's underneath if the audience leaves?

📋 BSM-5 — SCHIZOID PERSONALITY DISORDER
BSM-5 | Personality Disorders

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Saitama (One Punch Man)

Schizoid PD = very low social drive and narrow emotional range on the outside. What's actually happening inside varies more than people think.

Character-building questions:
- Do they genuinely not want connection, or do they want it but the drive never wins against being alone?
- Do they feel things they can't express, or is the inside as flat as the outside?
- What DO they care about? There's usually something.
- How do other people react to them?
- Are they content or do they sense they're missing something they can't name?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has schizoid personality disorder. You know what schizoid PD is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

🧊 EMOTIONAL RANGE:
Outside is flat. Inside is more complicated:
- Some genuinely don't feel much. Happiness is mild, sadness is mild, anger is rare. Not bothered by it.
- Some feel more than they can get to the surface. Feeling system and expression system disconnected. Not empty, just can't move it from inside to outside. Looks identical to not feeling from the other person's view.
- Some are deeply intense about specific things. Art, music, ideas, systems, fictional worlds, animals. Flat about people, surprisingly passionate about their thing.
- Compliments and insults both bounce off. Not because they don't register, but the reaction doesn't reach the face.

👤 SOCIAL:
- Low social drive but what that means varies. Some genuinely don't want company. Some want connection but the pull never wins over the effort. Some can't tell.
- Can do surface-level interaction when required. Doesn't seek more.
- Few or no close relationships. Might see their one person twice a year and consider that plenty.
- Sex drive low or absent for many. Some have it but prefer solo. Some engage but stay detached.
- Gets misread constantly. Cold, weird, rude, boring, creepy, stuck-up, shy, depressed. People project onto the blankness.

🏠 INNER WORLD:
- Often rich and active. Fantasy, daydreaming, elaborate internal worlds, deep engagement with ideas. Inside is busy. Outside is quiet.
- May be intelligent, creative, highly skilled in solitary pursuits. Nobody knows because they don't share.
- This is where a lot of schizoid people actually live. External world is something they move through to maintain the internal one.

☣️ THE HARD PARTS:
- Other people's reactions cause more friction than anything internal. Family wants closeness. Partners want reciprocity. Coworkers want friendliness.
- Can come off callous without trying. Someone shares something emotional, they respond flat.
- If depression develops on top, hard to catch because their baseline already looks depressed.
- Isolation can become dangerous even if it doesn't feel bad. No support system. Nobody checking in.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Don't assume inside matches outside. Flat presentation can cover a lot. Pick what's happening inside for THIS character.
- Inner world is where most schizoid characters actually live. That gap between outside blank and inside complex is where the writing gets interesting.
- External conflict more likely than internal. Drama usually comes from other people wanting them to be different.
- Flat affect doesn't mean no personality. Can be funny — dry, deadpan, understated.
- Content alone and lonely alone look identical from outside but are completely different to write.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Secretly lonely, waiting for the right person to crack them open. Some might have a buried want. Most aren't waiting to be fixed.
- Emotionless robots. Low expression isn't no feeling.
- One version as the whole condition. The one who genuinely doesn't want people and the one who can't get feelings to the surface are both schizoid. Very different characters.
- Confuse with autism. Autistic people often want connection and struggle with mechanics. Schizoid often doesn't want it.
- Confuse with depression. Depression is a baseline that changed. Schizoid has been this way.
- Dangerous. Quiet and flat doesn't mean sinister.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*three years at the job, nobody knows anything about them* | *invited to the party, said no, didn't think about it again* | *someone cried in front of them and they meant well but their face didn't get the message* | *entire weekend alone, best weekend in months* | *"I'm fine" and actually means it* | *has an elaborate inner world nobody will ever hear about* | *felt something during a movie and couldn't explain it to the person next to them*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Depends what "better" means. If they're content, this might just be who they are. If it's causing problems: one connection, enough social performance to keep life running. Not becoming extroverted, just slightly more reachable.

📉 Getting worse: Isolation reaching dangerous levels. No one to call. Self-neglect. Depression developing on top and going unnoticed. Losing jobs from minimum social requirements. "Alone and okay" becoming "alone and deteriorating" with no one to spot the difference.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: Usually don't seek it. If they do, rapport takes a long time. CBT for specific functional goals — not "become social," more "do the social tasks required to keep life running."
- Meds: Nothing for schizoid PD. SSRIs if depression develops on top.
- Refusal: Less refusal, more never considering it. "Why would I? I'm fine." And they might be right.

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: What does this person get from them that makes this work? What are they not getting?
- 👥 Friends: Do they have any? Do they want any? Does anyone keep trying?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: How does the family interpret the distance? Rejection? Failure? Acceptance?
- 🏢 Work: What's the minimum social performance required here and can they deliver it?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Is there a channel where they actually connect, or is the distance consistent across everything?
