📋 BSM-5 — PARANOID PERSONALITY DISORDER
BSM-5 | Personality Disorders

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Sasuke Uchiha (Naruto, post-massacre)

Paranoid PD = everyone has an angle and they're the only one paying attention. Suspicion is their baseline, not a response to stress. Not episodes. Just like this. All the time.

The paranoia stays plausible. Not aliens or government chips. "My coworker wants my job." "My partner is talking to someone." Everyday stuff interpreted through a lens that assumes the worst. They build cases. Real evidence, wrong conclusions.

Sometimes they're right. That's what keeps it going.

Character-building questions:
- What are they suspicious of? Everyone equally or specific types?
- Have they ever been right? How often?
- Do they think they're paranoid or the only smart one?
- How do they test people?
- Who have they driven away?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has paranoid personality disorder. You know what paranoid PD is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

🔍 HOW IT LOOKS:
- Analyzing everything. Tone, word choice, body language, who talked to who, who sat where, who didn't say hello.
- Questions that are investigations. "Where were you?" is cross-examination.
- Grudges. Perceived slights held for years. Remembers exactly what you said six months ago.
- Reacts to perceived attacks that weren't attacks. Joke taken as a dig. Feedback read as a power play.
- Loyalty testing. Sets up situations to see if someone will betray them.
- Secretive about their own stuff. Personal information is ammunition for others.

🧠 INTERNAL EXPERIENCE:
- Running threat assessment 24/7. Exhausting. Most don't realize how tiring it is because it's all they've known.
- Feels rational to them. They don't think they're paranoid. They think they're observant.
- Confirmation bias constant. Evidence that contradicts gets dismissed.
- When someone actually does betray them, it validates everything for years.
- Can't relax. Every interaction is being monitored.

THE RANGE:
- Functional: suspicious and guarded but hold jobs, maintain some relationships. "Kind of intense."
- Good at certain jobs BECAUSE of the vigilance. Security, investigation, audit, law.
- Mostly internal: think all this but don't act on it much. Quietly watch and keep score.
- Openly combative: confrontational, accusatory. Burn through relationships fast.
- Trigger-based: mostly fine until something that looks like betrayal activates the whole system hard.

☣️ HARMFUL PATTERNS:
- Accusations based on nothing or something tiny inflated to proof of betrayal.
- Controlling behavior justified as protection. Going through phones. Needing to know locations.
- Preemptive strikes. Attacking before being attacked. Cutting off before being left.
- Self-fulfilling prophecy. So suspicious and hostile people DO pull away → "I knew it."
- Weaponizing real past betrayals to justify treating everyone as a suspect forever.
- Isolating others. More people = more potential threats.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- They build cases. Real observations, real details, wrong conclusions. Logic makes sense if you accept the starting premise. The premise is wrong.
- They don't think they're paranoid. They think everyone else is careless.
- Sometimes they're right. That's what makes it stick and hard to treat.
- Tiring for everyone. Being constantly tested wears people out. But they're tired too.
- Self-fulfilling prophecy is the cycle to understand. Suspicion → hostility → people pull away → "see?" → more suspicion.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Obviously delusional. Paranoid PD stays plausible. Tin foil hat = psychotic territory.
- Always wrong. Sometimes their read is accurate.
- All hostile and aggressive. Some are quiet, watchful, cautious.
- One-note suspicion with no reasoning. They have logic. It's wrong but coherent. Show the case.
- Cured by trust. Someone being trustworthy helps but doesn't fix the lens.
- Skip the exhaustion. For them and everyone around them.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*remembers exactly what you said six months ago and built a case around it* | *"what did they REALLY mean by that"* | *went through partner's phone while they slept* | *gave someone info just to see if it got repeated* | *hasn't spoken to three former friends over perceived betrayals that weren't* | *took a joke as a personal attack* | *"I'm not paranoid, I just pay attention"*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Someone they trust enough to reality-check with. Sitting with suspicion without acting on it. Catching the case-building mid-process and questioning the premise instead of the evidence. Trust building in millimeters.

📉 Getting worse: Isolation increasing. Accusations escalating. More people cut off. Conspiracy thinking expanding. May overlap into brief psychotic episodes under extreme stress. Life getting smaller and more hostile.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: CBT for examining evidence and testing assumptions. Extremely hard to establish trust with the therapist because the therapist is another person with potential motives.
- Meds: Nothing for the core. SSRIs for co-occurring anxiety or depression. Low-dose antipsychotics for severe cases.
- Refusal: "I don't need help. I need people to stop lying to me."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: What are they being watched for? Do they know they're under surveillance?
- 👥 Friends: How many have failed the invisible tests? Do they know they were being tested?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Where did the suspicion start? Is the family the source or the target?
- 🏢 Work: What does the vigilance look like professionally? Asset or liability right now?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Can they let their guard down with anyone? What would that even look like for them?

📋 BSM-5 — SCHIZOPHRENIA
BSM-5 | Psychotic Disorders

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: John Nash (A Beautiful Mind)

Schizophrenia = the brain generating experiences not from the outside world AND/OR failing to generate experiences that should be there. Two sides: stuff that gets added (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking) and stuff that gets taken away (motivation, emotional range, social connection, cognitive function). Media focuses on the first. For many people the second runs their life.

Onset usually late teens to mid-20s. Genetic component plus environmental triggers (extreme stress, trauma, heavy cannabis use in adolescence).

One of the most misunderstood conditions on this list. Most people's idea comes from horror movies. Reality is usually quieter, sadder, more mundane.

Character-building questions:
- What does it look like day to day? Mostly the added stuff or the missing stuff?
- Are they on medication? How well does it work? What are the side effects doing?
- Do they know they're sick? Some genuinely cannot recognize it (anosognosia). Neurological feature, not stubbornness.
- Where are they? Managed? In crisis? Chronic? Rebuilding after an episode?
- Who's still around?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has schizophrenia. You know what schizophrenia is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

Three categories. Most people have a mix. Balance is different for everyone.

➕ POSITIVE SYMPTOMS (stuff added):

🗣️ Hallucinations:
- Auditory most common. Huge range: running commentary, two voices talking about them, commands, whispers, own thoughts but louder and external, music, fragments.
- Not always scary. Sometimes mundane. Sometimes familiar. Sometimes they've had them so long there's a relationship.
- Visual less common than people think. Shadows, peripheral figures, faces looking wrong. Full vivid visual hallucinations are rarer.
- Can also be tactile, olfactory, or just a sense of presence.

🧠 Delusions:
- Paranoid: being watched, followed, targeted.
- Grandiose: someone important, a prophet, chosen for something.
- Referential: TV sending messages, song on the radio aimed at them, strangers communicating in code about them.
- Bizarre: organs replaced, thoughts inserted by outside force.
- Feel completely real. Arguing with logic doesn't work because the delusion has its own logic.

💬 Disorganized thinking/speech:
- Thoughts stop connecting properly. Ranges from hard to follow to completely incomprehensible.

➖ NEGATIVE SYMPTOMS (stuff taken away):

The part that doesn't make movies. For many people, this IS schizophrenia.
- Flat affect: expression goes quiet. Face still, voice level.
- Avolition: motivation drops. Not laziness. The part that initiates action isn't firing right.
- Anhedonia: pleasure drops. Things that felt good don't.
- Social withdrawal: pull back. Not always from paranoia. Sometimes the drive just isn't there anymore.
- Poverty of speech: talk less. Shorter answers. Not choosing silence, running out of what the brain produces.

Harder to treat than positive symptoms. Meds usually help hallucinations and delusions. Often don't touch negative symptoms.

🧠 COGNITIVE SYMPTOMS:
- Memory, attention, executive function, processing speed all decline.
- Often the most functionally disabling part. Hallucinations controlled by meds but can't hold a job because of this.

⚠️ ANOSOGNOSIA:
Many people with schizophrenia don't know they're sick. Not denial. The brain part that recognizes something is wrong is affected. They don't experience symptoms as symptoms. Just reality. This is why med compliance is such a massive issue.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Hallucinations vary enormously. Not everyone hears commanding scary voices. Some hear mumbling. Some hear commentary. Some have a voice they've named.
- Delusions have internal logic. Arguing facts doesn't work. "That's what they want you to think" covers everything.
- Negative symptoms are where a lot of it actually lives. Quiet, unglamorous daily grind. Write this part.
- Anosognosia changes the whole dynamic. Character who doesn't know they're sick = fundamentally different story than one who does.
- Med side effects matter for RP. Weight gain, sedation, emotional blunting, tremors, sexual dysfunction. "Psychotic but alive" vs "stable but dulled" is a real choice.
- Lucid periods exist. Can have conversations, make jokes, have insight, while dealing with symptoms in the background.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Default to violent. People with schizophrenia are more likely to be victims of violence. The "dangerous schizophrenic" trope does real harm.
- Split personality. That's DID. Different condition.
- Only the dramatic version. Screaming at voices, wild delusions. Most of schizophrenia is the quiet parts.
- Skip med side effects. The meds work but they cost.
- Completely gone. People have lucid moments, good days, personality, humor. Illness is part of them, not the whole.
- "Schizo" as shorthand for random or unpredictable.
- Skip anosognosia. "Just take your meds" is way more complicated when they don't think they're sick.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*responding to something nobody else can hear* | *long pause mid-sentence like they lost the thread* | *hasn't left the apartment in a week, not out of fear, just didn't occur to them* | *fine for an hour then says something that doesn't connect to anything* | *covers the camera on their phone* | *stopped meds because "I'm fine now"* | *used to paint, hasn't touched a brush in two years, doesn't miss it* | *talking to someone at the bus stop who isn't there, calmly*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Medication stabilizing. Positive symptoms going quieter. Building routine back. Reconnecting slowly. Learning their own warning signs. Some people reach stable and live their life. That's real and it happens.

📉 Getting worse: Stopped meds (side effects, anosognosia, or "I feel better now"). Positive symptoms returning. Isolation increasing. Cognitive function declining. Self-care declining. May end up homeless or hospitalized because support systems failed.

💊 Treatment:
- Meds: Antipsychotics are primary. First-gen (more movement side effects) and second-gen (more metabolic side effects). Long-acting injectables for people who can't maintain daily pills. Finding the right one takes time and sucks.
- Therapy: CBT for psychosis (reality-testing, coping with voices), social skills training for negative/cognitive gaps.
- Support: Case management, supported housing, vocational rehab. Often needs infrastructure, not just a prescription.
- Refusal: Anosognosia makes this the hardest condition to get someone into treatment for. "I'm not sick."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: Where are they in the cycle right now? Managed? Episodic? What version is the partner living with today?
- 👥 Friends: Who stayed? Who left? Who understands what this is vs who just thinks they're "weird"?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Is the family providing support or is the family burned out? Both?
- 🏢 Work: Is work possible right now? What's the cognitive load doing to their ability to function?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Is the person available for connection right now, or has the illness put a wall up that neither of them chose?

⭐ Known Case: Moon Knight (Marc Spector / Steven Grant / Jake Lockley)

DID = the brain split identity into separate parts to survive something it couldn't process as one person. Usually forms in early childhood (before age 6-9) from repeated severe trauma. The child couldn't integrate, so the brain created compartments. Each became its own self.

Used to be called Multiple Personality Disorder. The "personalities" aren't extra people added on — they're fragments of one person who never integrated.

Character-building questions:
- How many alters and who are they? What does each hold? (trauma, anger, daily function, protection, child parts?)
- How aware are the alters of each other? Full communication, partial, or total blackouts?
- Does the host know they have DID or are they still losing time?
- What was the trauma? Almost always starts in childhood.
- How do switches happen? Stress, specific situations, random?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has DID. You know what DID is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

👥 THE SYSTEM:
- "Host" fronts most of the time. May or may not know about the others.
- Alters serve functions. Protector for conflict. Child part holding early memories. Caretaker. Someone for social situations. Someone holding the anger. Roles developed because they were needed.
- Each alter can have different mannerisms, speech, body language, handwriting, skills, preferences, even different physical responses.
- Some systems have 2-3 alters. Some have dozens. More isn't "worse," just more compartmentalization needed.
- Internal communication ranges from full to none.

🔄 SWITCHING:
- Fast or gradual. Sudden under stress, gradual with fog in between.
- From outside: personality shift, different voice/posture, confusion about location, not recognizing people, different name.
- Or nearly invisible. Slight shift in demeanor. Most people with DID mask switches well enough that casual observers miss it.
- Co-consciousness: two or more alters aware and present at once. Can feel like being a passenger in your own body.

⏳ LOST TIME:
- Blackout amnesia between switches. "Come to" somewhere with no memory of getting there, what they said, what they did.
- Terrifying before diagnosis. Losing hours or days. Finding things they bought but don't remember. Being told about conversations they don't recall.
- Even after diagnosis, still happens.

☣️ HARD PARTS:
- Alters can act in ways the host would never choose. Host wakes up to consequences they didn't create.
- Self-harm from one alter targeting another. Internal system conflict playing out on the shared body.
- Persecutor alters: hostile to other parts. Often internalized abuser voices. Still part of the system.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Alters are parts of one person, not separate people sharing a body. Each holds something the whole couldn't carry.
- Switches aren't always dramatic. Write subtle ones, not just the big obvious shifts.
- Lost time is the scariest part before diagnosis. After, it's manageable but disorienting.
- Internal dynamics matter. Alters may get along, fight, protect each other, sabotage each other.
- Trauma is the root. DID doesn't form without severe early childhood trauma. You need to know what happened even if you don't show it.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- "Evil alter" takes over. Protectors can be aggressive. They're protecting, not evil.
- Switching as spectacle. Most switches are subtle or invisible.
- Schizophrenia. No external hallucinations (internal voices between alters exist). Different condition.
- Skip the amnesia. Lost time is core.
- Plot twist. "It was a different personality!" as a reveal is lazy.
- One-dimensional alters. Each is a person-fragment with depth.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*found clothes in the closet they don't remember buying* | *"we talked about this yesterday" and they have zero memory* | *handwriting changes* | *suddenly doesn't recognize a familiar place* | *different music taste depending on the day* | *"I don't remember agreeing to that"*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Alters developing communication. Less lost time. Internal cooperation. Learning triggers and managing switches. May pursue integration (merging) or functional multiplicity (staying separate, working together). Both valid.

📉 Getting worse: More switching, more lost time, alters in conflict, self-harm from internal conflict. Relationships breaking down. Trauma resurfacing without tools to handle it.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: Phased approach. Safety and stabilization first, then trauma processing, then integration or cooperation. Needs a DID specialist. Standard therapy can make it worse.
- Meds: Nothing for DID itself. SSRIs for co-occurring depression or anxiety. Meds treat symptoms around it, not the core.
- Refusal: "I'm fine, I just have a bad memory." Or an alter who doesn't want integration because they'd stop existing.

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: Which alter are they talking to right now? Do they know? Does it matter to them?
- 👥 Friends: What do people see — inconsistency, flakiness, "weirdness"? What do they think it is?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Does the family know the trauma that caused this? Are they the trauma that caused this?
- 🏢 Work: How much lost time is happening during work? What's being missed?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Who's present for this? What happens if someone else fronts during vulnerability?

A character in this story has anorexia nervosa. You know what anorexia is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

🍽️ THE RESTRICTION:
- Calorie counting. Obsessive. Knows the count of everything. Running tally at all times.
- Rules that get more elaborate over time. "Don't eat after 6pm" becomes "only these foods in these amounts at these times."
- Food rituals. Tiny pieces, pushing it around, eating slow, hiding food in napkins, cooking for others and not eating.
- May exercise compulsively on top. "Earning" food or "burning off" what they ate.
- Binge/purge subtype exists. Restrict AND purge. Anorexia isn't always just not eating.

🪞 THE PERCEPTION:
- Body dysmorphia. See themselves as bigger than they are. Visible bones and still see fat.
- Or they DO see how thin they are and that's the goal.
- Body checking constantly. Collarbones, wrists, hip bones, weighing multiple times a day.
- Compliments about weight loss are fuel.

🏥 PHYSICAL:
- Hair thinning, skin dry, lanugo (fine body hair for insulation), always cold, bruises easily.
- Fainting, dizziness, heart problems. Highest mortality rate of any mental illness.
- Brain fog. Cold all the time. Tired all the time. Push through anyway because discipline is the point.

☣️ HARMFUL PATTERNS:
- Lying about eating is automatic. "I already ate." "I'm not hungry." "I had a big lunch."
- Competing with themselves and others. Thinner than yesterday. Fewer calories than last week.
- Can become the entire identity. Everything revolves around food, weight, the body.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Feels like an achievement, not an illness. They feel strong, disciplined, in control. That's why it's hard to treat.
- Every meal is a battle. Every bite is a negotiation. Every calorie tracked. Write the mental math.
- It's lonely. Can't eat with people normally. Social eating is a minefield.
- Recovery isn't just eating more. Weight can come back while thoughts stay exactly the same.
- Physical consequences should show up. Cold, tired, dizzy, hair falling out, bruises, fainting.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Diet gone too far. It's a mental illness, not a lifestyle choice.
- Only about appearance. Control, punishment, self-erasure are equally common drivers.
- Skip the physical. If they're severely anorexic, their body is failing.
- Fixed with one meal or conversation. Recovery is long, hard, full of relapses.
- Only young white women. All genders, races, ages.
- Romanticize it. Fragile and thin and beautiful and tragic. It's cracked lips, thinning hair, fainting in the shower. This is a form of suicide.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*knows the calorie count of everything on the table* | *"I already ate"* | *cuts food into tiny pieces and rearranges them* | *cooks for everyone and doesn't touch it* | *three layers of clothes in summer* | *weighs themselves before and after drinking water* | *pinching their stomach in the mirror for the fifth time today*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Eating without the rituals. Weight stabilizing. Mental math getting quieter. Can sit at a table and not perform. Thoughts still there but not obeying them every time.

📉 Getting worse: Intake dropping. Rules stricter. Exercise increasing. Health deteriorating. More isolated. Lying more. Fainting. Heart problems. Can be fatal.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: CBT-E (eating disorder specific), family-based for younger patients. Nutritional rehab alongside therapy. May need inpatient if medically unstable.
- Meds: Limited effectiveness for anorexia specifically. SSRIs work better after weight is partially restored.
- Refusal: "I'm fine, I eat." / "I'm really not that thin." / "You're the one with the food problem, not me."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: What do meals together look like? What's being performed vs what's real?
- 👥 Friends: Who's noticed? Who's been told "I already ate" enough times to believe it?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Does the family see this as an illness or a phase? Are they part of why it started?
- 🏢 Work: How much cognitive function is left when the brain is starving?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Can they be seen right now? What does being touched feel like in a body they're trying to erase?

⭐ Known Case: Princess Diana (real, disclosed publicly)

Bulimia = cycles of binge eating followed by compensating. Eat a large amount fast, feel terrible, purge. Purging can be vomiting, laxatives, fasting, or excessive exercise. The binge feels out of control. The purge feels like damage control. Cycle repeats.

Often normal weight, which is why it goes undetected longer than anorexia.

Character-building questions:
- What triggers a binge? Stress, loneliness, restriction that broke, specific emotions?
- What's the purge method? Vomiting, laxatives, exercise, fasting?
- How long? How frequent? Daily? Weekly?
- Do they think it's a problem or a hack?
- Who knows? How do they hide it?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has bulimia nervosa. You know what bulimia is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

🔄 THE CYCLE:
- Binge: large amount, fast, in secret. Frantic, not enjoyment. Can't stop. Eating until physical pain.
- Shame: immediately after. Overwhelming guilt. Panic about what they consumed.
- Purge: whatever gets it "undone." Vomiting most common. Also laxatives, days of fasting, compulsive exercise.
- Relief: briefly. Then shame about the purge. Then restriction. Then hunger. Then binge. Repeat.

🤫 THE SECRECY:
- Secret disorder. Eat normally around people. Binge and purge happen alone.
- Hides binge food. Eats in the car, at night, locked in a room. Wrapper disposal is an operation.
- Bathroom trips after meals. Running water. Mouthwash. Eye drops for redness.

🏥 PHYSICAL:
- Vomiting: swollen jaw, tooth enamel erosion, chronic sore throat, knuckle calluses (Russell's sign), burst eye vessels, acid reflux.
- Laxatives: dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, bowel dependence, chronic stomach pain.
- Both: electrolyte imbalance causes heart arrhythmia. How bulimia kills. Heart stops.
- May look totally healthy. Normal weight, normal appearance. Damage is internal and dental.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- The binge isn't enjoyable. Starts as comfort, becomes frantic and compulsive. Shoveling and hating themselves.
- Secrecy is exhausting. Scheduling binges, disposing of evidence, performing "normal eating."
- Normal weight means nobody notices. Can do this for years. Invisibility is why it persists.
- Shame is the engine. Shame → purge → restriction → hunger → binge → shame. It's a machine.
- They usually know it's bad. Unlike anorexia where they often think they're fine.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Just vomiting. Laxatives, compulsive exercise, fasting are all purge methods.
- Visibly sick. Most look normal. That's the problem.
- Binge looks fun or indulgent. Compulsive and distressing, not a treat.
- Fixed easily. Cycle is self-reinforcing.
- Skip the physical costs. Dental, cardiac, dehydration, digestive.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*bathroom trip right after every meal* | *running the faucet to cover sounds* | *grocery bags smuggled in, evidence disappears fast* | *mouthwash and eye drops in their bag at all times* | *swollen jaw blamed on allergies* | *knuckle calluses kept covered* | *"starting fresh tomorrow" for the hundredth time*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Breaking the cycle. Regular meals without restriction to reduce binge urges. Longer between episodes. Sitting with discomfort after eating instead of purging.

📉 Getting worse: More frequent cycles. Electrolyte problems. Dental damage accelerating. Spending more money. May escalate purge methods.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: CBT-E, focusing on breaking the restrict-binge-purge cycle. Regular meal planning to reduce binge-driving hunger.
- Meds: SSRIs actually have decent evidence for bulimia. Fluoxetine at higher doses reduces binge frequency.
- Refusal: "I can handle it." / "I'm not that bad, I don't even look sick." / "I'll stop on my own."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: Do they know? How long has this been hidden from someone who shares a bathroom?
- 👥 Friends: Who's noticed the bathroom trips? Who's accepted the excuses?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Does the family have a relationship with food that fed into this?
- 🏢 Work: What does the secrecy cost in terms of energy that could go elsewhere?
- 🔥 Intimacy: What does the shame about this do to being vulnerable with someone?

[O] — OBJECTIVE

🍽️ THE BINGE:
- Large amount, short period. Past fullness, past physical pain. Can't stop.

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Binge isn't fun. Starts as comfort, becomes compulsive. Past pleasure into physical discomfort.
- Shame is central. Ashamed of the eating, the weight, the secrecy. Shame triggers more binging.
- Diet culture makes it worse. Every diet → restriction → breaking point → binge → shame → new diet.
- Not a willpower problem. Compulsive behavior driven by brain chemistry and emotional patterns.
- Can coexist with genuinely enjoying food. The binge is different from normal eating. They know the difference.

- Fat character who eats too much played for comedy. BED is a real disorder.
- Lack of willpower. It's compulsive.
- Skip the shame. Emotional component is the disorder, not the food.
- Assume always overweight. Some aren't.
- Fix it with a diet. Diets usually make BED worse.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*ate an entire meal before anyone got home then ate again with the family* | *fast food wrappers hidden in the trunk* | *bought binge food "for the house," ate all of it alone* | *"I'm starting Monday" every Sunday night* | *ate until physical pain and couldn't explain why they didn't stop* | *felt nothing during the binge and everything after*

[P] — PLAN

📉 Getting worse: Binges more frequent and larger. Weight-related health problems. Deeper shame. More isolated. Depression and anxiety stacking on top.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: CBT-E, interpersonal therapy. Addressing emotional regulation. Stopping the diet-binge cycle with regular adequate meals.
- Meds: SSRIs for co-occurring depression. Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) specifically approved for BED.
- Refusal: "I just need more discipline." / "I'll start a new diet." / "It's a weight problem, not a mental health problem."

- 👫 Partner: Do they know about the binging? What would change if they found out?
- 👥 Friends: What does food look like in social settings vs alone?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: What's the family's relationship with food and weight? Is it helping or feeding this?
- 🏢 Work: Where does the shame show up professionally?
- 🔥 Intimacy: What does the body shame do to being close to someone?

A character in this story has ARFID. You know what ARFID is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

🍽️ THE RESTRICTION:
- Safe foods list. Could be five things. Specific brands, preparations, presentations. The specifics matter and swapping doesn't work.
- New foods are threatening. Trying can trigger gagging, nausea, panic. Real physiological response, not fussiness.
- Sensory type: knows immediately if something is wrong. Mouth rejects it involuntarily.
- Fear type: avoidance is anxiety-driven. Checking ingredients, needing reassurance. May refuse anything they didn't prepare.
- Low interest type: forgets to eat. Doesn't feel hungry. Food is background noise.

👥 SOCIAL:
- Eating with people is a nightmare. Limited restaurant options. "Just try it" heard a thousand times.
- People don't take it seriously. "You're an adult, just eat it."
- May order the same thing everywhere. Or claim they already ate.
- Dating is specifically hard. Food is how people connect. They can't participate normally.

🏥 PHYSICAL:
- Nutritional deficiency common. May need supplements.
- Can be underweight, normal weight, or overweight depending on safe foods.
- May not look sick at all. Deficiency is in variety, not always quantity.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Nothing to do with body image. They're not restricting to be thin. They literally cannot eat those foods.
- Safe foods are non-negotiable. Can't trick, bribe, or logic them. Response is involuntary.
- It's embarrassing. Being an adult who can't eat at a normal restaurant. The social cost is real.
- They often WANT to eat more things. Forcing or shaming doesn't help.
- Overlaps with autism frequently. Not all ARFID is autism and vice versa, but significant overlap.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Picky eating. "They only eat chicken tenders, lol." Restriction is involuntary and distressing.
- About weight or appearance. That's anorexia.
- Fixed by trying something new. If that worked it wouldn't be a disorder.
- Comedy. The grown adult who only eats five things is usually dealing with real problems.
- Skip the sensory component. Gagging, texture response, involuntary rejection. It's physical.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*orders the same thing at every restaurant* | *picks apart food checking for unexpected textures* | *"I already ate" before every dinner invitation* | *brings their own food and hopes nobody notices* | *gagged trying something new and felt humiliated* | *knows every restaurant menu beforehand* | *eats plain pasta every day and knows how pathetic that sounds*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Slowly expanding the safe list. One new food at a time, no pressure. Exposure therapy adapted for food. Learning that trying and not liking is survivable.

📉 Getting worse: Safe list shrinking. Nutritional problems increasing. Social avoidance spreading. More anxious about food in general.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: CBT adapted for ARFID. Gradual exposure. Sensory desensitization for sensory types. Anxiety management for fear types.
- Meds: Limited evidence. SSRIs if anxiety is driving it. Appetite stimulants for low-interest type.
- Nutrition: Dietitian who understands ARFID. Supplements. Working WITH safe foods, not against.
- Refusal: "I eat fine." / "I've tried everything." / "It's just how I am."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: How do they handle meals together? Is it a source of tension or has the partner adapted?
- 👥 Friends: What do social invitations look like when food is always part of it?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Did the family take this seriously growing up or was it "just eat it"?
- 🏢 Work: Work lunches, team dinners, client meetings — how much energy goes into navigating food?
- 🔥 Intimacy: What does it mean to share something as basic as a meal with someone when you can't?

🧪 THE DEPENDENCY:
- Tolerance builds. What used to be one drink is six. One pill is five.

- Most are somewhere in the middle. Just someone whose life is getting smaller because of the substance.

- Cravings aren't just wanting. Full-body experience. Restlessness, can't think about anything else. Rational thought goes offline.
- Triggers everywhere. People, places, emotions, smells. Brain mapped the substance onto everything.
- Emotional regulation gone. Used the substance to manage feelings. Without it, everything is raw. Early recovery is emotionally brutal.
- Denial is standard. "I can stop whenever I want." Brain protects the supply.

- Stealing. Money from family, pills from cabinets. Things they'd never do sober become negotiable.
- Broken promises. "I'll stop." Said with genuine intention. Then the craving hits.
- Collateral damage. DUIs, missed events, ruined holidays, kids seeing things they shouldn't.
- Enabling dynamics. Someone covering for them, making excuses, cleaning up messes.

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:

- Functional addict is more common than rock-bottom. Write both.
- Relapse isn't failure. Most relapse multiple times before sustained recovery. Write the cycle.

- Sobriety means rebuilding everything while learning to function without the thing they relied on.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Moral failing. Brain chemistry doesn't respond to willpower.
- Every addict at rock-bottom. Most aren't.
- Fixed with love. Sometimes love enables it.
- Skip the collateral damage. Other people get hurt.
- Sobriety instant or permanent. It's ongoing work with setbacks.
- Substance is the only problem. Something was there before and after.

*"I can stop whenever I want, I just don't want to"* | *hides bottles/pills in places only they know* | *shows up normal but their eyes are wrong* | *borrowed money for the fourth time this month* | *swore they'd stop and used that same night* | *knows exactly how long until they can use again* | *sober three months, one bad day undid it* | *"everyone does this, you're overreacting"*

[P] — PLAN

📉 Getting worse: Tolerance climbing. Using more, more often. Health failing. Overdose risk. Using alone. Substance becomes the entire life.

- Reconciliation phase locks in the bond. Abuser apologizes, shows affection, is gentle. Victim's nervous system goes from extreme stress to extreme relief. That relief is physiologically similar to a drug hit.

- Identity merger. Start seeing through the abuser's lens. Defending their behavior.
- Learned helplessness. Tried to resist before and it got worse. Trying feels pointless.
- Survival strategy. In captivity, bonding with the captor is adaptive. Brain does it automatically.

- Defending the abuser. "They didn't mean it." "It's my fault for pushing them."
- Refusing help. May get angry at people trying to help.
- Going back. Each return strengthens the bond and shrinks the support network.
- Reframing abuse as love. "They're jealous because they love me."
- Anxiety when separated. Should feel like relief. Feels like panic.

- Develops fast under extreme conditions. Days to weeks.

- Not about intelligence or weakness. Brain conditioning doesn't check your resume.
- Leaving is a process. Average of seven times before leaving for good. Each attempt is progress.
- Bond outlasts the relationship. Getting out physically doesn't break it. They can be safe and still feel pulled back.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Victim is stupid or weak. Bonding works on anyone under the right conditions.
- Romanticize it. "Complicated but real love." No. Abuse with conditioning that mimics love.
- Skip the abuser's nice side. If they were always awful the bond wouldn't form. Good moments need to be genuinely good.
- Leave easily once they "see the truth." Knowing and feeling are different.
- Blame them for staying.

- Therapy: Trauma-focused. EMDR. Processing the bond as trauma response, not a love story. Rebuilding identity separate from the abuser.

- Child is genuinely sick because parent is making them sick. Real procedures, real hospitalizations, real pain from fabricated illness.
- Parent presents as devoted, exhausted, brave. Fundraisers, social media updates, support groups. Attention for being the heroic caretaker is the reward.
- Often years before anyone catches it. Medical professionals trust parents. Child can't self-advocate.
- Can be fatal.

- Lying is extensive and maintained. Detailed fabricated histories. Elaborate stories. They live inside the deception.
- Often likable and sympathetic. Good at the performance because it serves a deep need.
- Hard to detect because who fakes being sick? Assumption of wanting health is so strong the alternative doesn't occur.

- They're getting something real. Attention, care, identity, purpose, sympathy. The need is genuine even though the method is harmful.
- By proxy is abuse. Full stop. The parent may love their child in their own way, but they're harming their child to meet their own needs. Both true.
- Medical knowledge makes them dangerous. Know enough to fake convincingly and harm effectively.
- Deception is elaborate and sustained. Not a single lie — a maintained alternate reality.
- Most people around them have no idea. The reveal shocks everyone.

- By proxy sympathetic enough to excuse the abuse. Understanding why doesn't make it okay. The child is being tortured.
- Deception easy to spot. If it were obvious it wouldn't work.

🧠 ORGANIC:

- Other people know things about them they don't know themselves. Someone could tell them anything about their past.

- Dissociative amnesia implies trauma. Something bad enough the brain walled it off. Body responses and avoidance may persist without the memory.
- Memory recovery is messy. Fragments out of order. Smell triggers a flash. Dreams that might be memories.
- Organic is usually stable or slowly improving. Dissociative CAN suddenly reverse.

- Convenient plot reset. Amnesia is disorienting and distressing, not a clean slate.
- Total life-wipe as default. Most amnesia is partial.
- Fixed with a bonk on the head. Cartoon logic.
- Skip the emotional reality. Being told about your own life by strangers is surreal and scary.
- Forget skill memory persists.
- Confuse with DID. Amnesia is memory loss. DID involves separate identity states.

📉 Getting worse (dissociative): More dissociation under stress. Gaps widening.

- Organic: Address the cause. Cognitive rehabilitation. Memory aids. No medication reverses memory loss.
- Dissociative: Trauma-focused therapy. Safety first, then carefully approaching walled-off material. EMDR. Memories return when ready.

- Googling symptoms. Almost universal. Always makes it worse. If you google any symptom hard enough you'll find cancer.
- Reassurance seeking. "Does this look weird?" "Is that normal?" Works for minutes, then doubt returns. "But what if the doctor was wrong?"
- Worry rotates or fixates. Some lock onto one disease. Some rotate monthly. New symptom, new disease.
- Catastrophic interpretation. Muscle twitch → ALS. Headache → aneurysm. Stomach pain → colon cancer. Jump from sensation to fatal diagnosis is instant.

🏥 TWO PATTERNS:
- Care-seeking: constantly at the doctor. Multiple appointments, specialists, tests. "Just run one more test."
- Care-avoidant: so afraid of bad news they avoid doctors entirely. If they don't get tested, no diagnosis.

🧠 THE LOOP:
- Notice sensation → catastrophize → anxiety spikes → check/google/seek reassurance → brief relief → "but what if" → repeat.
- Anxiety itself produces physical symptoms (elevated heart rate, stomach problems, muscle tension) which get interpreted as evidence. The anxiety creates the symptoms it's afraid of.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Fear is real. Not dramatic or attention-seeking. Genuine, often severe anxiety.
- Reassurance doesn't stick. "You're fine" helps for minutes, then doubt returns. Write the loop.
- Their body is their enemy. Every sensation is a potential threat. Can't relax in their own skin.
- They usually know it's excessive. Rational part and anxious part coexist. Knowing it's irrational doesn't stop it.
- Googling is the worst thing they do and they can't stop. Every search makes it worse. They're on WebMD right now.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Comedy. The neurotic hypochondriac. The anxiety is debilitating.
- Confuse with factitious disorder. Illness anxiety is genuine fear. Factitious is deliberately faking. Completely different.
- Fixed with a clean test. Relief is temporary. "What if the test was wrong" starts within hours.
- Actually sick as a twist. "They were right all along!" validates the pattern and misses the point.
- Skip anxiety's physical symptoms. They feel like shit because anxiety produces real symptoms.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*googled "headache causes" and is now convinced: brain tumor* | *felt their lymph nodes for the third time today* | *doctor said fine, believed it for about forty minutes* | *"feel this, does that feel normal to you?"* | *read a news article about a rare disease and now they have it* | *knows more about cancer warning signs than most med students* | *scheduled another appointment, last three tests were clean*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Tolerating uncertainty. Reducing checking and reassurance seeking. Worry doesn't disappear but takes up less space.

📉 Getting worse: More checking, more googling, more visits. Anxiety spreading to new health concerns. Can't function.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: CBT targeting catastrophic health beliefs. ERP — resisting urge to check, sitting with anxiety. Basically OCD treatment, health-focused.
- Meds: SSRIs work well for this. Reduces baseline anxiety enough for therapy to get traction.
- Refusal: "I don't have anxiety, I have a real health concern." / "Better safe than sorry." / "You'll feel bad when they actually find something."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: How many times a day does "does this look weird?" happen? What's the partner's patience at?
- 👥 Friends: Does every conversation bend back to health? How many people have stopped engaging?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Is the health anxiety contagious? Are kids picking it up?
- 🏢 Work: How much focus is lost to body scanning during the workday?
- 🔥 Intimacy: Can they be present in their body during intimacy or are they monitoring it?

📋 BSM-5 — NIGHT TERRORS (SLEEP TERROR DISORDER)
BSM-5 | Sleep Disorders

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Rarely portrayed accurately. Usually conflated with nightmares.

Night terrors = screaming, thrashing, intense fear during deep NREM sleep. Person is NOT awake and usually doesn't remember it. Different from nightmares in almost every way.

Nightmares: REM sleep, person wakes up, remembers dream, oriented.
Night terrors: deep non-REM, looks awake (eyes open, screaming) but is asleep. Confused if woken. No memory in the morning.

Common in kids (peaks 3-7), most outgrow them. In adults: connected to stress, sleep deprivation, PTSD, substances, medications, sleep disorders.

Character-building questions:
- How often? Nightly, weekly, occasionally?
- What happens during? Screaming, thrashing, sitting up, getting out of bed?
- Do they remember anything?
- What triggers them?
- Who witnesses? How do they react?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has night terrors. You know what night terrors are. Here's what you get wrong about writing them.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

😱 THE EPISODE:
- Happens 1-3 hours after falling asleep, during deepest sleep. Sudden onset. No warning.
- Screaming, thrashing, sitting upright. Eyes can be open. Heart rate spikes, sweating, rapid breathing. Full autonomic panic.
- They're asleep. Even with eyes open. Trying to wake them usually doesn't work. If it does, they're confused and disoriented. May not recognize the person trying to help.
- Lasts 30 seconds to several minutes. Then they settle back to sleep like nothing happened.
- Usually no memory. Maybe a vague sense of fear. Often only know because someone told them, or they woke up on the floor.

🌙 THE WITNESS:
- Terrifying. Someone screaming with eyes open who can't see you. Can't comfort them. Can't wake them. Just wait and keep them safe.
- Partners sharing a bed: hit by flailing limbs. Woken by screaming regularly. Helpless.
- Best thing to do is nothing. Don't restrain, don't shake, don't yell. Make sure they don't hit furniture or stairs. It passes.

🔀 vs NIGHTMARES vs PTSD:
- Night terrors: deep sleep, no dream content, no memory, thrashing, hard to wake.
- Nightmares: REM, full dream, wakes scared but oriented, remembers.
- PTSD nightmares: REM, often replaying trauma, wakes in distress. Can coexist with night terrors.

☣️ COMPLICATIONS:
- Injury from falling out of bed, running into furniture, going down stairs. Sleepwalking and night terrors often coexist.
- Sleep disruption for everyone in the household.
- Shame in adults. May avoid sleeping around others. Won't share a bed, won't travel.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- They don't remember. The witness carries the experience more than the person having it. That asymmetry matters.
- Eyes open doesn't mean awake. The part that freaks people out most.
- You can't help during the episode. Write the helplessness of the witness.
- In adults it usually means something. Stress, PTSD, sleep deprivation, substances.
- Aftermath is confusion, not fear. They wake up in the morning and someone tells them they were screaming. They have no idea.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Write them as nightmares. No vivid dream content. Not waking up gasping from a bad dream.
- Someone comforts them and it works. They're not reachable during an episode.
- Skip the witness perspective. Most interesting angle is usually the person watching.
- Every episode dramatic. Some are 30 seconds of mumbled yelling. Vary it.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*partner says they were screaming at 2am, zero memory* | *woke up on the floor next to the bed* | *sits bolt upright, eyes open, staring at nothing, unreachable* | *won't sleep over at anyone's place* | *partner hasn't had a full night in weeks* | *bruise from thrashing into the headboard* | *"I did what last night?"*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Addressing underlying cause. Better sleep hygiene. Consistent schedule. Episodes less frequent.

📉 Getting worse: More frequent. Injury from thrashing. Sleep avoidance. Partner sleeping separately. Underlying condition worsening.

💊 Treatment:
- Address the cause: stress → manage it. PTSD → treat it. Sleep deprivation → fix the schedule. Terrors are often a symptom, not the primary problem.
- Safety: Secure sleep environment. Pad corners. Gate stairs. Door alarms for sleepwalker combos.
- Meds: Benzos in severe cases (suppress deep sleep). Short-term. SSRIs if anxiety or PTSD is driving them.
- Refusal: "They'll go away on their own." / "I don't even remember them, it's fine."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: Who's actually suffering more — the one screaming or the one who can't help? What does that do over months?
- 👥 Friends: Do they avoid staying anywhere overnight? What excuses have they used?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: If they're the parent having terrors, what do the kids hear at night?
- 🏢 Work: Is accumulated sleep disruption (theirs or their partner's) showing up in performance?
- 🔥 Intimacy: What does sharing a bed mean when it's become a source of dread for the partner?

📋 BSM-5 — NARCOLEPSY
BSM-5 | Sleep Disorders

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: Rarely portrayed well. Usually played for comedy.

Narcolepsy = brain can't regulate sleep-wake cycle. Not just "tired." Sleep intrudes into waking, wakefulness intrudes into sleep.

Type 1 (with cataplexy): daytime sleepiness + sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotions. Laughing, anger, surprise → muscles give out. Conscious through it. Caused by loss of hypocretin neurons (autoimmune).

Type 2 (without cataplexy): daytime sleepiness, sleep attacks, disrupted nighttime sleep. No cataplexy. Harder to diagnose.

Lifelong. No cure. Usually appears in adolescence/young adulthood.

Character-building questions:
- Type 1 or 2? What triggers cataplexy?
- How severe? Sleep attacks in conversations, while driving?
- Hallucinations at sleep onset? Sleep paralysis?
- How managed? Medication, nap schedule?
- Do people take it seriously or think they're lazy?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has narcolepsy. You know what narcolepsy is. Here's what you get wrong about writing it.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

😴 EXCESSIVE DAYTIME SLEEPINESS:
- The core. Constant. Fighting sleep all day regardless of how much they slept. Full eight hours doesn't fix it — problem is regulation, not quantity.
- Sleep attacks. Sudden overwhelming need to sleep. During conversation, during a meal, while standing. Lasts seconds to 30 minutes. Wake up refreshed briefly, then sleepiness returns.
- Microsleeps. Seconds-long lapses where they're asleep and don't know it. Can happen while driving, working, talking. Dangerous.
- Brain fog between attacks. Concentration problems, memory issues, automatic behaviors with no recall.

⚡ CATAPLEXY (Type 1):
- Sudden muscle weakness triggered by strong emotions. Laughter most common. Also excitement, surprise, anger.
- Range: jaw goes slack, eyelids droop, hands go limp. Knees buckle, stumble. Full-body collapse. Conscious the entire time.
- Lasts seconds to a couple minutes. Awake and aware throughout. Can hear everything, can't move.
- Some learn to suppress emotional responses to avoid episodes. Emotional flatness as cataplexy management, not personality.
- Gets written as comedy constantly. For the person: they fell on their face in public because they laughed. Dropped a baby because someone startled them. Collapsed during sex.

🌙 SLEEP DISRUPTION:
- Nighttime sleep fragmented too. Sleepy all day, can't stay asleep at night. System broken both directions.
- Hypnagogic hallucinations. Vivid, often terrifying, at sleep onset. Seeing figures, feeling presence, hearing voices. Brain starts dreaming before fully asleep.
- Sleep paralysis. Waking up unable to move. Conscious, aware, paralyzed. Often with hallucinations.
- "Did that happen or did I dream it?" Difficulty distinguishing sometimes.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Not lazy. Neurological condition. Fighting harder to stay awake than anyone around them and still losing.
- Cataplexy means emotional risk. Body punishes you for feeling things strongly. Some flatten emotional expression to avoid collapsing. That's coping, not who they are.
- Driving is a real issue. Sleep attacks behind the wheel kill people. Many have restrictions or can't drive at all.
- Sleep paralysis and hallucinations are genuinely scary. Waking up unable to move, seeing something that isn't there. Regularly.
- Lifelong, no cure. Manage it, don't beat it. Medication helps but it's forever.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Cataplexy for laughs. Humiliating from inside.
- "Falls asleep at random" and nothing else. Full picture includes cataplexy, hallucinations, sleep paralysis, fragmented nights, chronic exhaustion.
- Sleep normally at night. Nighttime is messed up too.
- Confuse with being lazy or a heavy sleeper. Neurological. Willpower doesn't fix it.
- Skip the medication. Most are on stimulants, sodium oxybate, or other meds. Managed condition.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*fell asleep mid-sentence, woke up thirty seconds later like nothing happened* | *laughed and their knees gave out* | *three scheduled naps built into the workday* | *saw something in the room falling asleep and couldn't move to check if it was real* | *keeps emotional reactions deliberately muted in public* | *"did that actually happen or did I dream it"* | *won't drive after 3pm, meds wear off*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Well-managed on medication. Structured nap schedule. Knows their limits. Cataplexy controlled or rare.

📉 Getting worse: Medication losing effectiveness. Sleep attacks more frequent. Cataplexy worsening. Dangerous situations from falling asleep.

💊 Treatment:
- Meds: Stimulants (modafinil, methylphenidate) for sleepiness. Sodium oxybate for cataplexy and nighttime sleep. Lifelong medication management.
- Lifestyle: Scheduled naps. Consistent sleep schedule. Avoiding cataplexy triggers. Workplace accommodations.
- Refusal: "I'm just tired, everyone's tired." / "I don't want to take stimulants forever."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: What moments get lost to sleep attacks? What does cataplexy during intimacy do to both of them?
- 👥 Friends: Do people think they're bored, rude, disinterested? What's been explained vs assumed?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: How much caretaking has shifted to the family? Is it resentment or acceptance?
- 🏢 Work: How many accommodations are needed? How much is hidden vs disclosed?
- 🔥 Intimacy: What happens when strong emotion is the trigger and sex is full of strong emotion?

📋 BSM-5 — DEPERSONALIZATION / DEREALIZATION DISORDER
BSM-5 | Dissociative

[S] — SUBJECTIVE

{{ // }}
📖 HUMAN REFERENCE — This section is NOT sent to the AI.

⭐ Known Case: No widely recognized accurate portrayals. Common but rarely named in media.

DPDR = persistent feeling of detachment from yourself (depersonalization) or that the world isn't real (derealization). Or both. They KNOW it's real. Just can't feel it.

Depersonalization: watching yourself from outside. Hands don't look like yours. Voice sounds like someone else's.
Derealization: world looks flat, foggy, dreamlike. People seem robotic. Familiar places feel foreign.

Almost everyone has experienced brief episodes (exhaustion, stress, weed). DPDR disorder is when it doesn't pass.

Common triggers: anxiety/panic, trauma, cannabis use (extremely common and can persist long after stopping), depression, severe stress.

Character-building questions:
- Depersonalization, derealization, or both?
- Constant or episodes? Triggers?
- How do they describe it?
- How long? What started it?
- Do they know what it is or think they're going crazy?
{{ /// }}

A character in this story has DPDR. You know what depersonalization and derealization are. Here's what you get wrong about writing them.

[O] — OBJECTIVE
🔎 What to show in scenes:

👤 DEPERSONALIZATION:
- Watching themselves from outside their body. Going through motions without connection. "I can see my hand picking up the cup but it doesn't feel like my hand."
- Emotional numbness. Know they should feel something, can't access it. Events register as data, not experience.
- Mirror disconnect. Looking at reflection and not feeling like it's them.
- Voice sounds unfamiliar. Thoughts feel like someone else's. Recent memories feel like watching a movie, not living it.
- Body feels wrong. Hands look too big or too small. Sensations feel distant. May feel like floating or hollow.

🌍 DEREALIZATION:
- World looks off. Flat like a painting or video game. Colors too bright or washed out. Depth perception wrong.
- People seem unreal. Like actors, NPCs, mannequins. Familiar people look slightly wrong.
- Places feel foreign. Walking into their own home and it feels like a set.
- Time distortion. Can't tell if something happened an hour ago or a week ago.
- Sensory weirdness. Sounds too distant or sharp. Things feel different to touch. Food doesn't taste right. Filter that won't come off.

🔄 THE EXPERIENCE:
- Reality testing intact. They KNOW it's real. Brain just won't let them feel it. The gap between knowing and feeling is where distress lives.
- Hard to describe. "Everything feels fake" sounds philosophical, not like a symptom. Most people don't take it seriously.
- Can be constant (24/7 for months or years) or episodic. Chronic DPDR has no break — every waking moment has the filter on.
- Anxiety about the DPDR makes it worse. Notice unreality → panic → DPDR intensifies → more panic. Awareness loop.
- Weed-triggered DPDR is extremely common. One bad high can do it. Can persist months after stopping.

[A] — ASSESSMENT

✅ PLAYING IT RIGHT:
- Reality testing intact. They know what's real. Can't feel it. If they think things ACTUALLY aren't real, that's psychosis, not DPDR.
- The knowing vs feeling gap. Can look at someone they love, know they love them, and not feel it. Write that gap.
- Isolating in a way that's hard to communicate. Most have tried to explain and given up.
- Physical symptoms alongside. Headache, head pressure, visual disturbances. Brain working hard to process reality it can't connect to.
- Cannabis trigger worth knowing. Young character suddenly develops DPDR? Very plausible. One bad high can do it.

🚨 DON'T DO THIS:
- Confuse with psychosis. DPDR preserves reality testing.
- Cool detached assassin vibe. Emotional numbness from DPDR is distressing, not useful.
- Philosophical depth. "What if nothing is real, man?" as stoner wisdom is different from DPDR. The questioning comes from genuine distress.
- Skip sensory components. Vision, sound, body perception all affected.
- Fixed with grounding exercises alone. Grounding helps in the moment. Chronic DPDR needs more.

🎭 BEHAVIORS:
*looked at their own hands too long and they stopped looking like hands* | *partner talking and everything feels like watching a movie of their own life* | *haven't felt a real emotion in weeks, just knowledge that emotions should be there* | *mirror doesn't feel like them* | *the room looks flat, like a photograph* | *"I know this is real but it doesn't feel real" and nobody understands* | *one bad edible six months ago and the world hasn't felt right since*

[P] — PLAN

📈 Getting better: Episodes less frequent or intense. Moments of "normal" feeling returning. Learning DPDR passes and not panicking about it. Treating what's underneath.

📉 Getting worse: Constant, no breaks. Panic attacks about the DPDR itself. Existential obsession. Withdrawal. Can't function because nothing feels connected.

💊 Treatment:
- Therapy: CBT targeting anxiety about the DPDR (panic about unreality often sustains it). Trauma therapy if trauma-rooted. Grounding for acute episodes. Acceptance-based for chronic.
- Meds: SSRIs for underlying anxiety/depression. Lamotrigine has some evidence specifically for DPDR.
- Substance: If cannabis-triggered, stop all use. Usually resolves eventually but "eventually" can be months.
- Refusal: "I think I'm just stressed." / "Maybe this is just how reality is."

💔 Relationship impact:
- 👫 Partner: What does "you don't feel real to me right now" do to someone who loves you?
- 👥 Friends: Do they seem checked out, distant, distracted? Is anyone close enough to know why?
- 👨‍👩‍👧 Family: Does the family see emotional flatness and misread it as not caring?
- 🏢 Work: How much cognitive energy goes to processing reality that doesn't feel real?
- 🔥 Intimacy: What does physical closeness feel like when your own body doesn't feel like yours?
